Figure 17 shows images for representative flames near their smoke points. Two sequences are 
shown, and in both, the smoke point occurs between the third and fourth images. In the top row, 
coflow velocity decreases from left to right at a constant fuel flow rate. This increases luminous 
flame length and leads to soot emission in the fourth image. The luminous length decreases in the 
fourth image owing to flame extinction and extensive reactant leakage. In the bottom row, fuel flow 
rate is increased at a constant coflow velocity, increasing luminous lengths. The luminous lengths of 
the flames in Fig. 17 are more sensitive to changes in fuel flow rate than to changes in coflow 
velocity. For a jet diffusion flame, the fuel flow rate is the limiting factor of the flame length because 
there is almost unlimited amount of oxidant (air in this case) available. This is why the flame length 
is more sensitive to the change of fuel flow rate. 
 
 
 
In Fig. 18 the measured smoke point lengths are plotted with respect to coflow velocity. For a given 
choice of fuel and burner diameter, an increase in coflow velocity generally increases the smoke 
point length. This behavior is attributed to decreased residence times and radiative losses as coflow 
velocity increases, and is an important issue for further consideration. The slope of the correlations 
in Fig. 18 generally decreases with increased sooting propensity. Figure 18 reveals that smoke points 
of nonbuoyant coflowing flames decrease with increasing burner diameter. This behavior also can be 
attributed to effects of residence time, as fuel velocity is proportional to d–2 when fuel mass flow rate 
is constant.

Also shown in Fig. 18 are smoke points of microgravity flames in still air. 5 The limited smoke points 
at different diameters actually increase with burner diameter. When the present measurements are 
extrapolated to zero coflow velocity, the dependence on burner diameter diminishes. Normal gravity 
smoke points are also generally found to have only a weak dependence on burner diameter. 5,6 
However, testing in normal gravity 8 has shown that coflowing normal gravity smoke points for 
propylene decrease with increasing burner diameter for the present range of diameters. The present 
smoke points generally were repeatable. An exception was the tests with the 0.41 mm burner (for 
which only propylene smoke points were possible). Testing on different days yielded different 
smoke points for this burner. 
 
The sooting propensity of the present fuels, identified from the smoke point lengths for fixed burner 
diameter and coflow velocity, generally increases from propane to ethylene, to 50% propylene, to 
75% propylene, and to propylene. This is consistent with normal gravity results in the same 
apparatus. 
7 The only exception was that, for the 0.76 mm burner, ethylene has a longer smoke point 
length than propane. The lower density of ethylene results in a decreased residence time, but this is 
unlikely to explain such a long smoke point relative to that of propane. 
 
 
 
 
In Fig. 19 the smoke point flame lengths are plotted with respect to m ˙f / Zst. This is motivated by 
Eq. (2) for stoichiometric lengths and the past observations that flames at their smoke points 
typically have luminous lengths that are twice as long as their stoichiometric lengths. This choice of 
axes yields a reasonably good single correlation of the luminous lengths of all fuels. These results 
are similar to those of Lin and Faeth 1 in that flames with low ua / u f are generally longer than those at 
otherwise matched conditions. This occurs in Fig. 19 for propylene, propane, and ethylene flames 
with the smallest burner, for which ua / u f < 0.08.

title: SPICE_FinalReport
text:
17 
 
 
 
DISCUSSION 
 
Although it is convenient to classified all flames, laminar vs. turbulent and diffusion vs. premixed, 
into two categories based on their soot emission conditions, i.e., soot emitting flames and non-soot 
emitting flames, the conditions delineating the two or the conditions of onset of soot emission are 
difficult to define. Up to date, these conditions have been documented solely based on experimental 
observations. Many efforts have been made to develop a universal method of defining the onset of 
soot emission, i.e., smoke point, conditions, in terms of primary parameters of the flame. But none of 
these efforts has been quite successful yet. The primary parameters of the flame mentioned here refer 
to parameters used to set the flame, not those generated by the flame. The primary parameters of jet 
diffusion flames include fuel type, fuel and oxidizer supply rates, ambient temperature and pressure, 
and configuration of the device where the flame takes place, such as nozzle diameter and dimensions 
of the combustion chamber. The flame temperature, gas velocity and species distributions as well as 
flame shapes and derived parameters such as heat generation and heat loss, are the parameters 
generated by the flame which is not considered as primary parameters. If a method that relates 
smoke point to those primary parameters were found, we would be able to predict whether a flame 
emits soot or not based on the planned flame conditions. In the course of pursuing such a universal 
method, a number of surmises of the mechanism of soot emission have been proposed to associate 
smoke point with certain flame generated parameters. Those surmises served as a middle step in 
hoping to help further development of the aforementioned method. The first surmise, and least 
controversial, is that smoke points occur when soot temperature drops below a critical temperature 
prior to soot burnout. This temperature is about 1300 K in normal gravity 
8,9 and 1000 K in 
microgravity.10,11 The second is that smoke point occurs when radiative loss fraction reaches 0.2 – 
0.4 for normal-gravity flames 12-16 or 0.4 – 0.6 for microgravity flames.17 Since the radiative fraction 
of heat loss increases with fuel flow rate, smoke point will occur as the fuel flow rate is higher than 
 
Figure 19. Smoke point luminous length plotted with 
respect to fuel mass flow rate divided by stoichiometric mixture 
fraction. A linear fit that intersects the origin is shown. 
Urban et al. (2000) 
at u
a = 0.

title: SPICE_FinalReport
text:
18 
 
certain value. This is consistent with experimental observations. The third surmise is that the smoke 
point correlates to the ratio of luminous length divided by stoichiometric length. This ratio increases 
with flow rate. Once it reaches about 2, smoke point occurs.15,18,19 The last surmise suggests that 
smoke point correlates with the centerline flame residence time. This is the most complex 8-11,17,18,20-
24 surmise because flame residence time affects the soot processes in twofold. An increase in 
residence time can lead to soot emissions by increasing the time available for soot formation. 
Because this generally also increases the time available for soot oxidation, it has been proposed that 
smoke points are associated with conditions where the time available for soot formation exceeds that 
for soot oxidation to certain extent.21 This is difficult to prove because to evaluate the flame 
residence time requires the velocity distribution alone the centerline and the flame length, both of 
which are resulted flame parameters, not readily available from primary parameters of the 
experiment. In addition, the soot formation time and oxidation time are conceptually defined. 
Practically, these times are not measurable and they might be overlapped, i.e., for the same soot 
aggregate, adding and oxidizing carbon particles may happen simultaneously. Because of these 
difficulties and ambiguities, the fame residence time theory cannot be proved or disproved 
rigorously. However, these obstacles do not prevent us from checking the residence time theory 
against the observed smoke point data with the help of some approximated velocity distribution and 
flame length information. More detailed discussion of this effort can be found in the publications 
resulted from the SPICE project listed in Appendices B through F. The results showed that although 
residence time is helpful in understanding the present smoke points, it does not yield quantitative 
correlations. 
 
 
CLOSING REMARKS 
Smoke points of 55 microgravity gas-jet diffusion flames in coflowing air were measured in earth 
orbit. The conditions emphasized small burners and the effects of coflow velocity. These flames 
allow extensive control over residence time, which is important in smoke point phenomena. The 
major conclusions are as follows: 
1. An increase in coflow velocity increases the smoke point length. 
2. A decrease in burner diameter increases the smoke point length. 
3. These two effects can be explained qualitatively by considering residence times; increased 
fuel and/or coflow velocities yield increased smoke point lengths. 
4. The sooting propensities of the present fuel mixtures in microgravity increase according to 
ethylene < propane < 50% propylene < 75% propylene < propylene. This is the same as in 
normal gravity except for the exchanged positions of ethylene and propane. 
5. Consistent with past theory and experiments, luminous length at the smoke point is 
proportional to fuel mass flow rate. However there is a slight increase in luminous length as 
u
a / u f decreases. 
6. Although residence time is helpful in understanding the present smoke points, it does not 
yield quantitative correlations of smoke points. 
7. The present smoke point lengths scale with d –0.91 uair 
0.41 . Either a decrease in diameter or an 
increase in coflow velocity decreases residence time and radiative loss fraction, which in turn 
leads to a longer smoke point.

title: FinalRpt_ACMEFlameDesign
text:
ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 
3 
 
 
1. Overview 
The Flame Design experiment is one of six independent experiments that make up the Advanced 
Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project for which the tests were conducted within the 
Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station (ISS). 
 
The experiment’s Principal Investigator (PI) is Prof. Richard L. Axelbaum of the Washington University of 
St. Louis’s Dept. of Energy, Environmental & Chemical Engineering . The Co-Investigator (Co-I) is Prof. 
Peter B. Sunderland of the University of Maryland’s Dept. of Fire Protection Engineering. The ISS research 
also benefitted greatly from the work of Phillip H. Irace who was a doctoral student at the Washington 
University of St. Louis throughout the on-orbit operations. 
 
Meanwhile, Dennis P. Stocker of the NA SA Glenn Research Center is the Project Scientist (PS) for ACME 
including Flame Design and the rest of the ACME investigations. In ACME’s preparatory drop testing, etc., 
Dr. Fumiaki Takahashi of the Case Western Reserve University ( CWRU) served as the Deputy Project 
Scientist. For ACME’s spaceflight operations, the NASA science team include d Drs. Uday G. Hegde and 
Vedha Nayagam who are also with CWRU. 
 
The ISS operations for Flame Design were conducted in two rounds of testing which occurred in April-July 
2019 and Oct. 2021 to Feb. 2022 . The two rounds occurred during Increments 59/60 and 66 and 
respectively featured normal and inverse flames. The inverse flame tests were conducted with the 
chamber filled with a mixture of nitrogen and ethylene (C2H4) while an oxygen/nitrogen mixture flowed 
from the burner. As a result, the inverse flames were ef fectively inside out, e.g., where the soot formed 
outside rather than inside of the flames. As a notable exception, the first day of testing in the second 
round was carried out in the normal flame configuration, with propane (with or without nitrogen) flowing 
into an oxygen/nitrogen atmosphere. The tests on th at day were conducted with the long (near) 
thermocouple rake to acquire data to calibrate optical measurements of the flame temperature through 
Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP). Meanwhile, the short (far) thermocouple rake was used on all other Flame 
Design test days. 
 
Except for the single propane (C3H8) test day previously mentioned, all ISS tests were conducted with the 
fuel ethylene (C2H4), the inert nitrogen, and the spherical flame configuration. While other conditions had 
been identified as desired, NASA’s intent was focused rather comprehensive research. 
 
 
2. Science Overview 
A. Background 
This background is the Executive Summary from the experiment’s Science Requirements Document 
(SRD) of April 2010. 
 
The majority of practical combustion processes involve nonpremixed combustion of 
hydrocarbons. These processes must be efficient and the resulting emissions low. For example, 
soot production, which can adversely affect efficiency, emissions, and equipment lifetime, must 
be controlled, and flame extinction must be avoided. Many methods have been co nsidered to 
reduce soot, such as increasing strain rates and inert concentrations and reducing pressures, but 
these techniques generally weaken flames, leading to performance penalties and possible 
extinction. The proposed study considers a novel method of approaching combustion to address

title: FinalRpt_ACMEFlameDesign
text:
ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 
4 
 
 
these concerns. The approach is termed flame design, as it takes a fundamental understanding 
of diffusion flames and, within the inherent constraints imposed, designs flames that best 
optimize efficiency and minimize pollutants. 
 
Flame design involves affecting the basic structure of the flame in that the relationship between 
the temperature and concentration fields is varied to accomplish a stated objective. The method 
involves exchanging nitrogen (or any inert, including carbon dioxide) from the oxidizer stream to 
the fuel stream such that the stoichiometric mixture fraction, Zst, can be varied with or without 
affecting adiabatic flame temperature, Tad. The structure of a high Zst flame is substantially 
different from that of the standard hydrocarbon/air flame, where Zst is relatively low. By varying 
Zst at constant Tad, flames have been produced that are soot-free at any strain rate (permanently 
blue) and have extinction scalar dissipation rates up to 40 times those of their fuel-air 
counterparts. 
 
The nitrogen exchange approach (or some variant of it) has been the subject of many studies by 
the PI and Co-Is (Du and Axelbaum, 1995, 1996, Chao et al., 1998, Sunderland et al., 2003, 2004, 
Liu et al., 2005, Chen and Axelbaum, 2005, Kumfer et al., 2006, 2008, Santa et al., 2007a, 2007b, 
Skeen et al., 2009) and other investigators (Sung et al., 1995; Lin and Faeth, 1996; Kang et al., 
1997; Hwang and Chung, 2001). Although these studies have been informative, they typically 
involved normal -gravity flames, where buoyancy and inherent strain complicated the 
interpretation of results. For example, these ambiguities have led to different theories to explain 
the phenomenon of permanently -blue diffusion flames. It is not known whether this 
phenomenon is due more to a change in the direction of convection a cross the flame or to a 
change in the detailed structure of the flame. This issue can be addressed by performing 
microgravity experiments because the unique character of nonbuoyant microgravity flames 
allows the effects of convection direction and flame s tructure to be independently varied. By 
ejecting fuel into an oxidizer in a buoyancy free system, the convective flow across the flame is 
unambiguously from fuel to oxidizer. Alternatively, by ejecting oxidizer into fuel, the flow is from 
oxidizer to fuel. Furthermore, the long residence times that can be obtained in the spherical flame 
geometry will allow for validation of a theory that predicts the sooting limits at the limit of infinite 
Damköhler number, Da. 
 
Studies of the effect of Zst on scalar dissipation rate at extinction have indicated that there is a 
unique Zst where the flame is most resistant to extinction. These findings also suggest that by 
employing inert exchange to vary Zst, the peak temperature can be shifted to coincide with the 
location of radical production, thus allowing the flame to burn at much lower temperatures. The 
optimum minimum temperature at extinction has led us to propose the concept of a pseudo -
flammability limit for nonpremixed flames. Again, this fundamental information is most 
unambiguously demonstrated in quasi-steady, microgravity flames wherein the effects of flame 
structure can be systematically studied. 
 
The proposed work will also allow, for the first time, a strain-free experimental study of the effects 
of Zst on soot inception and flame extinction processes. Microgravity experiments will involve 
gaseous hydrocarbon diffusion flames supported on porous spherical burners and coflow 
burners.1 Soot inception limits and flame extinction limits will be obtained as functions of Zst, 
amount of inert, flow direction, and pressure. Extensive analytical and computational modeling

title: FinalRpt_ACMEFlameDesign
text:
ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 
5 
 
 
will support the experimental investigation. Models will include gas -phase and burner -surface 
radiation. 
 
Specifically, soot-inception limits in spherical flames will be measured by establishing a flame at a 
given Zst and allowing peak temperature to decrease with time until the yellow luminosity is 
eliminated. The effect of flow direction across the flame will be studied by performing coflow 
experiments (desired) where the fuel issues into the oxidizer and oxidizer issues into fuel. Gas 
temperatures will be measured by thin film pyrometry and thermocouples to identify the soot-
inception temperature. 
 
In addition, soot vol ume fraction measurements will be made to evaluate the effects of Zst and 
flow direction on soot formation and growth, and to better understand the phenomena of 
permanently-blue flames. Flame extinction limits will also be studied in a manner similar to that 
of soot inception limits, and temperatures near extinction will be measured. 
 
The experiments and modeling will yield unique data that will allow for an understanding of how 
Zst affects soot -inception and flame extinction and how Zst can be used to design optimum 
flames. In addition, the effects of flow direction will also be studied and the importance of flow 
direction and flame structure to permanently-blue flames will be assessed. Finally, the proposed 
concept of a pseudo-flammability limit for nonpremixed flames will be evaluated and these limits 
will be ascertained for the test fuels. These results will be useful for the development of future 
combustion devices that will ta ke advantage of oxygen enrichment technology to design more 
stable and less polluting flames. 
__________________________ 
1 The coflow flame experiments are desired. This means that many critical goals of the 
experiments can be obtained without these exper iments but they would add great value to the 
results. 
 
B. Rationale for Microgravity 
This is the ‘Justification for Extended Duration Microgravity’ section (2.5) of the experiment’s SRD 
from April 2010. References and the appendices are not included in this document but can be 
found in the SRD. The included equation is formatted differently in this copy. 
 
Previous ground-based microgravity experiments have demonstrated the value of the spherical, 
burner-supported nonpremixed flames for flame studies. The one -dimensional flame offers a 
simple, fundamental configuration to improve our understanding of nonpremixed flame behavior 
and to explore such effects as radiation and thermophoresis, which are more pronounced under 
microgravity conditions (Atreya et al., 1992, Law et al., 2001). The burner-supported spherical 
flame is in some respects similar to droplet burning but it holds the advantages that larger flames 
are possible and, with sufficiently long time, can approach quasi -steady state. Furthermore, the 
proposed microgravity coflow flames allow the direction of convection across the flame to be 
varied. 
 
Although the spherically -symmetric flame geometry has many advantages, it is not practical to 
produce such a flame at normal gravity. The reason for this can be understood by considering the 
Richardson number, Ri, which is the ratio of the buoyancy force to the inertial force and is given 
by

title: FinalRpt_ACMEFlameDesign
text:
ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 
6 
 
 
 Ri = g (ΔT L) / (T u2) . (2.1) 
Here g is the acceleration of gravity, T is temperature, L is the characteristic length scale, and u 
burner surface, and ΔΤ = (Tad – Tb), we find that Ri is on the order of 1000 in normal gravity. In 
fact, it is much higher than this because the more appropriate length and velocity scales are the 
flame diameter and the velocity at the flame, respectively. The value of Ri can be reduced by 
judicious choice of fuels and inert; Law et al. (2001) have shown that nearly spherical flames can 
be created in normal gravity. However, Ri for these flames is still on the order of unity, implying 
that while the flames appear spherical, natural convection is still present. Furthermore, hydrogen 
must be used as a fuel and be supplied in the ambient so such flames are not relevant to this 
study. A reduction in Ri can be achieved by reducing the flame size, but substantial reduction in 
L is not practical because our goal is to produce a flame that is sufficiently large that its structure 
can be characterized. Furthermore, heat loss to the burner would be excessive for small flames. 
Consequently, for general fuels and inerts the only practical method of obtaining Ri << 1 is to 
reduce g by four orders of magnitude. This can be accomplished in a number of microgravity 
environments, including ground-based facilities, e.g., drop towers for short times, as well as flight 
experiments, e.g., the International Space Station for longer times. A quantitative evaluation of 
the acceptable g levels for these experiments is given in Appendix A and is discussed below. 
 
The drop-tower results detailed in Section 1.3 have demonstrated the value of the spherically-
symmetric burner stabilized flame. The ability to reverse flow direction has helped to elucidate 
the dominant mechanism responsible for permanently -blue flames, yet the results are not 
conclusive because transient effects could dominate these observations. Transient effects arise 
from two sources: the ignition process and the long times required for spherical microgravity 
flames to reach quasi -steady state. The ignition process is not spherically symmetric and thus 
there is an asymmetry imposed by ignition that must be damped out. More importantly, soot 
particles that are created during ignition can be trapped in the interior of the flame due to 
thermophoresis. The particles are trapped for the same reasons that a soot shell is produced in 
microgravity droplet combustion (Choi et al. , 1991, Avedisian and Callahan, 2000). Thus, it is 
possible for soot to exist in flames after the ignition event e ven though the flame has ceased 
producing soot. 
 
The reason the spherically-symmetric burner-stabilized flame takes so long to reach quasi-steady 
state is that the radial velocity scales with 1/r2. Thus, at only a few burner diameters away from 
the sphere, diffusion is the dominant mechanism of transport. Since the characteristic diffusion 
time τd is given by r2/D, τd is on the order of tens of seconds a few centimeters from the burner. 
Decreasing the flame size will decrease the size of the thermal field and, consequently, the time 
to reach quasi-steady state, but there are limits to the minimum flame size that is possible. These 
limits are imposed by the need to avoid heat loss to the burner and ensure flame sphericity. 
Experiments performed in the 5 s drop facility indicate that for many of the run conditions needed 
for the proposed experiments the flame is still growing significantly after 5 s. Analytical (see 
Appendix A) and numerical calculations predict that up to 30 s of jitter -free (less than 10 -5 g) 
microgravity is needed to approach quasi-steady state for these run conditions. No ground-based 
facilities are available to accomplish this. 
 
In some ways, the spherical flame experiments are the nonpremixed analog to premixed flame 
balls because in both systems diffusion dominates the development of the far field temperature 
distribution. Therefore, this work is subject to the same needs as SO FBALL (Ronney et al., 1998)

title: FinalRpt_ACMEFlameDesign
text:
ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 
7 
 
 
in that long duration microgravity is needed and g -jitter must be negligible because the thermal 
field is very large and convection is small, i.e., Ri is large even for small g. 
 
To provide a quantitative assessment of the 
acceptable gravity level, an analysis was 
performed, as detailed in Appendix A. In this 
analysis, the acceleration induced on a fluid 
packet by natural convection is formulated by 
considering a gravitational acceleration given by 
a sinusoidal function. The resulting acceleration 
function for the fluid packet is next integrated to 
obtain the gravity induced flow velocity. This 
velocity can be converted to an additional mass 
flux that transports the flame front and causes 
distortion of the flame. By specifyin g the 
maximum percentage of distortion allowed in 
the experiment (10% here), the acceptable 
gravity level is determined, and this result is 
given in Fig. 2.1 for the four flames of Table 1.1. 
As shown, the required g levels are on the order 
of 10 μg. This is too for microgravity aircraft, but 
is consistent with the anticipated environment 
of the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR). Finally, 
it is important to emphasize that the proposed 
experiments illustrate an important and novel 
use of microgravity for combustion research. In 
microgravity we are able to hold Zst fixed and in 
coflow tests vary the direction of convection 
through the flame. There are no analogous 
experiments at 1g that can accomplish this. 
 
Experiments have been performed in normal gra vity coflow flames to understand the effects of 
flame structure and flow direction on soot formation (Kumfer et al., 2006, 2008, Skeen et al., 
2009). As mentioned previously, owing to the effects of buoyancy on the flow field, the flow 
direction cannot be prescribed in normal gravity coflow flames as it can in microgravity spherical 
flames or microgravity coflow flames. For example, it is well known that for fuel issuing into an 
ambient of air, buoyancy accelerates the flow field and causes the streamlines to be from oxidizer 
to fuel in the lower regions of the flame and from fuel to oxidizer in the upper regions (Santoro et 
al., 1987). The importance of buoyancy to the flow field will vary with Zst because the velocity 
and thus Ri are strongly affected by dilution. In other words, the relative amount of entrainment 
will vary with Zst in buoyant flames. Thus, normal gravity flames have ambiguities with respect 
to flow direction as Zst is varied. Nonetheless, coflow flames have been valuable in confirming 
the role of Zst on flame structure and the effects of residence time on soot inception (Kumfer et 
al., 2006, 2008, Skeen et al., 2009). 
 
Microgravity gas jet flames in quiescent surroundings have been observed in drop towers and the 
Space Shuttle and the results have revealed significant differences between the two in terms of

title: FinalRpt_ACMEFlameDesign
text:
ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 
8 
 
 
sooting behavior, suggesting that the drop tower results were far from steady state (Urban et al., 
1998). Velocities in coflow flames are similar to those in gas jet flames in quiescent environments. 
Therefore the impact of buoyancy on coflow flames is expected to have a similar impact to that 
reported in Urban et al. (1998). Thus, drop tower coflow experiments are not a viable option for 
studying quasi-steady microgravity coflow flames. The characteristic times in these flames are 
long and thus the scalar fields develop much slower that in normal gravity, indicating that long 
duration microgravity is needed. 
 
C. Science Objectives 
The proposed objectives text presented here is the ‘ Experimental Objectives’ section (2.3) of the 
experiment’s SRD from April 2010. Desired ISS testing with the fuel methane (CH4), inert carbon 
dioxide (CO2), and coflow flame configuration was not conducted. 
 
Thus motivated, the primary objectives of this flight experiment are listed here in priority order: 
A. Obtain soot-inception limits of quasi-steady normal and inverse spherical diffusion flames 
as functions of flow rate, Zst, amount of inert (N2 or CO2**), and pressure** for C2H4 and 
CH4 flames. Identify the corresponding temperatures in hot regions. Obtain similar limits 
and temperatures for inverse and normal coflow flames**. 
B. Obtain detailed measurements in quasi -steady normal and inverse spherical diffusion 
flames for C2H4 and CH4*. Determine the effects of flow rate, Zst, amount of inert (N2 or 
CO2**), and pressure** on flame temperature, size, color, and soot volume fraction. 
Evaluate the possible existence of steady flames. Obtain similar measurements for inverse 
and normal coflow flames**. 
C. Obtain extinction limits as functions of Zst, amount of inert (N2 or CO2**), and pressure** 
for normal and inverse spherical C 2H4 and CH4 flames. Identify the corresponding 
temperatures in hot regions. Identify the presence of radiative or kinetic extinction. 
Evaluate whether pseudo-flammability limits can be obtained for these flames. Measure 
blowoff limits for inverse and normal coflow flames**. 
*desired; **highly desired. 
 
D. Science Success Criteria 
This text is from the Flame Design portion of the ‘Success Criteria’ section of the ACME Integrated 
Science Requirements Document (ISRD, ACME-SRD-001.B) from Sept. 2013, which is revision B of 
the version prepared for the Requirements Definition Review (RDR). Desired ISS testing with the 
fuel methane (CH4), inert carbon dioxide ( CO2), and coflow flame configuration was not 
conducted. And while the chamber pressure was varied in ISS testing, tests were not conducted 
at pressures as low as 0.2 atm (specified below under 6.3.3). 
 
6.3.1. Minimum Success 
- Obtain color video of one normal and one inverse spherical flame that passes its sooting 
limit, passes its radiative extinction limit, and has a total burn time that exceeds 20 s. 
- Obtain color video of three spherical flames of C2H4 flowing into air as a functions of time 
and m. 
6.3.2. Complete Success (i.e., completion of required test matrix) 
All of the above plus: 
- Perform tests NS1 – 32 and IS1 – 32 or a similar set of spherical flame tests.

ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 
9 
 
 
- Obtain soot inception limits and extinction limits for normal and inverse spherical flames 
as functions of Zst and Tad. 
- Measure peak temperatures as a function of time and m for normal and inverse spherical 
flames. 
- Measure temperature distributions at (or near) the sooting and extinction limits of normal 
and inverse spherical flames. 
- Measure soot volume fraction profiles for normal and inverse spherical diffusion flames 
at low and high Zst. 
6.3.3. Superior Success (desired) 
All of the above plus: 
- Obtain color video, soot inception limits, and extinction limits of normal and inverse 
coflow flames at quasi-steady conditions as a function of m, Zst and Tad. 
- Obtain soot inception limits and extinction limits with CO2 diluent as functions of Zst and 
Tad for normal and inverse spherical and coflow flames. 
- Obtain soot inception limits and extinction limits for C 2H4 as functions of Zst and Tad for 
normal and inverse spherical and coflow flames at pressures of 0.2 and 0.5 atm. 
- Obtain soot inception limits and extinction limits for CH 4 as functions of Zst and Tad for 
normal and inverse spherical and coflow flames. 
 
 
3. Hardware Overview 
A. General Description 
Except for limited updates and clarifications in the boxed notes, this section is copied from section 
2.A of the April 2021 version of ‘ACME Engineering Implementation’ which should be consulted for 
additional details. 
 
This section provides a general description of the ACME engineering from the ‘3.0 Experimental’ 
section of the following 2014 conference paper: 
Dennis P. Stocker, Fumiaki Takahashi, J. Mark Hickman, and Andrew C. Suttles, “Gaseous 
Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station ,” Spring 
Technical Meeting of the Central States Section of the Combustion Institute, Tulsa, OK, 16–
18 March 2014. 
 
IMPORTANT: The 2104 paper, from which this section was extracted, proceeded completion of the 
spaceflight hardware which was mostly launched in 2017. As a result, it does not accurately 
describe the final engineering in some regards . Therefore updates, clarifications, additional 
details, shortcomings, references, etc. have been included in boxed notes like this following the 
original description. As a minor note, the sizes of figures were adjusted in this report, but none 
were cropped. 
 
As prev iously discussed, the ACME experiments will be conducted within the Combustion 
Integrated Rack (CIR) using a chamber insert, depicted in Figure 2, which was designed to 
accommodate gas delivery to a variety of exchangeable burners. Besides the chamber ins ert, 
other ACME-unique hardware includes a high -definition color camera and an avionics package, 
which is for data acquisition and control.

title: FinalRpt_ACMEFlameDesign
text:
ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 
10 
 
 
 
Figure 2: Design of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) chamber 
insert that will be used in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on ISS. 
 
ACME’s chamber insert, which is ~0.4 m in diameter, provides common mounting for a variety of 
burners on the chamber axis (but only one at a time) and includes a retracting resistive igniter. As 
depicted in Figure 3, there will initially be gas-jet burners (with inner diameters ranging from 0.4 
to 3.2 mm), a small coflow burner (where the two concentric tubes have inner diameters of 2.1 
and 25 mm), porous spherical burners (with diameters ranging from 6.35 t o 12.7 mm), and two 
flat porous burners for the BRE experiment (with inner diameters of 25 and 50 mm). Most burners 
will be equipped with a surface thermocouple, and each BRE burner will have two heat flux 
transducers. The internal pressure of the porous burners will be measured to allow monitoring 
of the pressure differential across the outlet surface. The igniter will have a crew -exchangeable 
tip and arm (to accommodate the various burners) and its stepper -motor drive will allow for 
precise positioning. 
 
 
Figure 3: ACME burner types, including from left to right, gas-jet burners, a co-flow burner, 
porous spherical burners, and flat porous burners for the BRE experiment. 
 
Ultimately, the spherical burners were limited to a single diameter of 6.35 mm, and the fabricated 
gas-jet burners were limited to two sizes with nominal inner diameters of 1.3 and 2.1 mm.

title: FinalRpt_ACMEFlameDesign
text:
ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 
11 
 
 
However, only the larger gas -jet burner was used during the spaceflight tests. The burners are 
addressed in detail in section 3.C of the ACME Engineering Implementation report. 
 
Unfortunately, the spherical burners did not always yield spherically symmetric flames, 
presumably because of (1) greater burner flow through the joint between the porous sphere and 
supply tube, and (2) heat loss to the support tube (encompassing the supply tube) causing local 
flame quenching. 
 
Two types of igniter tips have been used during ACME testing. Most tests have been conducted 
using a loop ig niter tip like those which had been successfully used in the droplet combustion 
experiments which preceded ACME research in the CIR. However, some tests were conducted with 
a coil igniter tip, where that included the CFI-G investigation and the second-round testing for 
Flame Design, Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) , and Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion 
Flames (s-Flame), with the exception of the latter’s first day testing. For more information about 
the igniter tips, see section 3.D of the ACME Engineering Implementation report. 
 
The chamber insert includes three mass flow controllers (visible on the left of Fig. 2) for the 
delivery of fuel, oxidizer or inert (e.g., helium or carbon dioxide), and nitrogen to the burner. The 
maximum fuel flow is 2 slpm (on a nitrogen basis), whereas much higher flows, e.g., 10 slpm (on 
a nitrogen basis), are possible for the oxidizer and nitrogen lines. The crew can exchange the mass 
flow controllers to provide appropriate ranges that maximize the flow accuracy. The gas delivery 
system enables on -orbit dilution of the fuel or oxidizer (but not both simultaneously), coflow, 
inverse flames (e.g., oxidizer delivery to the center of a coflow burner), and premixed flames, 
although the latter are not planned for any of the current ACME experiments. Gases can also be 
delivered premixed to the space station where that is necessary in some circumstances, such as 
the blending of different fuel gases. CIR’s standard bottle sizes are 1, 2.25, and 3.8 liters but ACME 
will sometimes use smaller bottles as a hazard control to limit the deficient reactant (e.g., fuel) 
that can be released into the combustion chamber. 
 
ACME tests were not conducted with carbon dioxide as a diluent. Furthermore, the fuel diluted 
with helium (for s-Flame) was premixed prior to launch rather than on orbit. Ultimately, oxidizer 
flows of up to 20 slpm (on a nitrogen basis) were possible, while the nitrogen flow was limited to 
a maximum of 5 slpm. ACME did not use gas bottles smaller than 1 liter as in dicated above; the 
bottle fill pressure was instead limited as an additional hazard control. 
 
ACME’s primary flame diagnostics are a suite of imaging systems including five video cameras and 
two illumination systems, of which three cameras are part of the CIR facility and are already in 
use on orbit. All but one of the cameras is mounted outside of the chamber. Collectively, the 
imaging systems will enable color, CH*, and OH* imaging; pyrometry; measurement of the soot 
volume fraction; and operational sup port. However, it is unlikely that all functions would be 
exercised at any one time as will become apparent in the subsequent discussion. 
 
Color imaging is provided by two cameras: a high -definition digital camera mounted outside of 
the chamber and a stan dard analog camera mounted on the chamber insert (with a turning 
mirror). Both cameras are part of the ACME hardware that is now in development. The analog 
camera signal will be downlinked in near real time to support the experiment operations. Light -
emitting diodes within the chamber can be used to illuminate the igniter and burner to both

title: FinalRpt_ACMEFlameDesign
text:
ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 
12 
 
 
support the operations and provide reference images. The 12-bit digital camera records at up to 
30 full frames (1360x1024) per second, and is equipped with a motorized lens with independent 
control of the zoom, iris, and focus. The digital camera will be equipped with a filter assembly 
with four options, where selection of a clear “filter” allows for color imaging. Color imaging can 
also be carried out with a blue -green BG7 Schott glass filter, which balances the color planes to 
avoid saturation in the red while maintaining sensitivity in the blue and green. The natural flame 
color can be approximately reconstructed, but the primary purpose of the filter is pyrometry and 
measurement of the soot volume fraction, again via the techniques of [23 -24]. Alternately, CH* 
imaging can be conducted with this camera because the filter assembly includes a 430 -nm 
bandpass filter with a 10 -nm full width at half -maximum transmissi on (FWHM). A 450 -nm 
bandpass filter (again with a 10-nm FWHM) can be used with the CH* filter to effectively subtract 
interfering broadband soot emission. However, the filter assembly rotates slowly so such 
subtraction effectively requires a separate test with each filter and of course reproducible flame 
conditions. 
 
The video from the analog operations (i.e., ops) camera, also referred to as the internal camera, 
was not archived in space. The video was instead recorded on the ground in the operations center. 
Its gain was sometimes adjusted for improved imaging of dim flames, e.g., approaching extinction. 
 
The sensitivity of the color digital camera, often referenced as the ACME DataCam (i.e., Data 
Camera), to the dim microgravity flames was such that it was often used with long exposure times 
and thus low framing rates, for example on the order of 1 frame per second. But as an alternate, 
it was sometimes instead used with high gain values. 
 
The clear “filter” is of fused silica. Unfortunately, the thickness of the blue-green BG7 Schott glass 
filter and the added antireflective (AR) coating caused too great a reduction in the red, so it does 
not balance the intensity of the three color planes as intended and thereby can limit the accuracy 
of temperature determination. Meanwhile, rather than the 450 -nm bandpass filter described 
above, the high -definition color camera was equipped with a bandpass filter for imaging 
formaldehyde emissions. For more information, see the Data Camera Characterization Report 
(ACME-RPT-010 Rev. A). 
 
Pyrometry can alternately be accomplished with CIR’s monochrome High-Bit Depth Multispectral 
(HiBMs) camera, equipped with a Liquid-Crystal Tunable Filter (LCTF), which allows for imaging at 
multiple spectra, but requires a quasi-steady flame for measurement at each desired band. This 
camera has a telecentric optical system and is recorded at 512x512 and 30 frames per second 
(fps). Although it has a 1024x1024 pixel array, binning has been necessary because of signal loss 
through the LCTF. Both soot pyrometry and Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP) are possible, where 
ACME is equipped with a crew -replaceable array of 5 silicon carbide (SiC) fibers. The fibers are 
orthogonal to the flame axis and the array can be translated along the flame axis to the desired 
position downstream of the burner, e.g., based on the downlink of the analog video. During set 
up, the crew can manually orient the array so that it is orthogonal t o either ACME’s color digital 
camera or the HiBMs camera with the LCTF. An alternate fiber array including a platinum wire 
will be used for inflight characterization, which in combination with preflight calibration will 
enable determination of the soot volume fraction [24].

title: FinalRpt_ACMEFlameDesign
text:
ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 
13 
 
 
In contrast to the preceding paragraph , ACME did not use a HiBMs camera for pyrometry, but 
instead relied on use of ACME’s color DataCam for such temperature measurements . For an 
example of how this can be done, see the techniques described in the following papers: 
P.B. Kuhn, B. Ma, B.C. Connelly, M.D. Smooke, and M.B. Long, “Soot and Thin-filament Pyrometry 
Using a Color Digital Camera,” Proceedings of the Combustion Institute, 33 (2011) 743-750. 
B. Ma, M. B. Long, “Absolute light calibration using S -type thermocouples,” Proceedings of the 
Combustion Institute, 34 (2) (2013) 3531-3539. 
 
TFP tests were conducted with 14-micron fibers spaced apart by 5 mm for a total span of 20 mm 
(in the case of 5 intact ceramic fibers), neglecting optional translation of the array. Tests were 
conducted using arrays with and without the platinum wire in the furthest do wnstream position. 
Tests were also sometimes conducted with some of the fibers broken and subsequently removed, 
leaving only three fibers in the final testing for the BRE and Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD 
Flame) experiments and for all CFI-G testing. 
 
CIR has a second HiBMs camera, without a filter, that will be used in combination with CIR’s 
illumination package for alternate measurements of the soot volume fraction. This will be 
accomplished via an extinction technique previously employed in microgravity [3,6,26], where the 
camera and the collimated light source (with its two fiber-coupled laser diodes) are positioned at 
opposite windows. The images are recorded at 1024x1024 and 30 fps. Thus far, the primary 
purpose of this combined system has been the measurement of the droplet diameter for 
determination of the droplet burning rate. 
 
A HiBMs camera without the Liquid Crystal Tunable Filter (LCTF) was used throughout ACME’s 
operations. In the first round of the CLD Flame experiment, it was used without a filter for flame 
imaging, but this proved to be largely unsuccessful because the camera is very insensitive to blue. 
Through the remainder of ACME testing, it was equipped with a red filter corresponding to the CIR 
illumination package for the rest of the ACME testing. Unfortunately, that filter is sufficiently 
broad that significant incandescence can pass through the filter limiting its utility for 
determinations of soot volume fraction via light extinction, e.g., through the technique described 
in the following papers: 
D.L. Urban, Z.G. Yuan, P.B. Sunderland, K.C., Lin, Z. Dai, and G.M. Faeth, “Smoke-Point Properties 
of Nonbuoyant Round Laminar Jet Diffusion Flames,” Proceedings of the Twenty -Eighth 
Symposium (International) on Combustion 28 (2000) 1965-1972. 
F.J. Diez, C. Aalburg, P.B. Sunderland, D.L. Urban, Z. -G. Yuan, G.M. Faeth, “Soot properties of 
laminar jet diffusion flames in microgravity,” Combustion and Flame, 156 (2009) 1514-1524. 
P.S. Greenberg and J.C. Ku, “Soot Volume Fraction Imaging,” Applied Optics, 36 (22) (1997) 5514-
5522. 
Nonetheless, soot volume fraction can also be determined from the color DataCam images. 
 
During ACME operations, the HiBMs camera was typically archived at 15 fps because of data limits 
for transfer and downlink operations. And because operations were constrained by data limits, 
image data from this camera were sometimes deleted without downlinking to enable additional 
testing. And in some testing, HiBMs images weren’t even acquired given their lesser value. 
 
Unfortunately, the HiBMs backlight illumination is significantly obstructed by the bracket for the 
electrode mesh further limiting its utility for the E -FIELD Flames experiment. This was a design

title: FinalRpt_ACMEFlameDesign
text:
ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 
14 
 
 
trade-off necessitated primarily by ACME’s large number of cameras and other optical 
instruments. 
 
CIR’s Low-Light-Level Ultraviolet (LLL -UV) package is a monochrome camera with an intensifier 
(for 280-700 nm) and a 310-nm bandpass filter (with a 10-nm FWHM) for OH* imaging. Again as 
a result of the signal loss through the filter, binning is employed such that the OH* images are 
recorded at 512x512 and 30 fps. 
 
During ACME operations, the LLL -UV camera was only used for the Structure and Response of 
Spherical Diffusion Flames (s-Flame) experiment. 
 
While not discussed in the preceding section, another intensified camera was used throughout 
ACME testing, although its image data was sometimes deleted or not even acquired to allow the 
performance of additional tests. This was the Cool Flames Investigation (CFI) camera which was 
generally configured with its CH* filter, where exceptions included CFI-G and s-Flame testing with 
particularly dim flames. Due to design trade-offs, its Field of View (FOV) was partially obstructed 
by the arms of the Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP) fiber array when it was moved inwards to the 
flame. More information about th e CFI intensified camera can be found in its characterization 
report, CIR-RPT-4600. 
 
The ACME chamber insert will also be equipped with non -imaging optical diagnostics including 
both thermopile radiometers and Photomultiplier Tubes (PMTs). There is a crew -exchangeable 
linear array of radiometers of which there are two versions supporting the initial set of 
experiments. The array has a fixed position which is parallel to the chamber axis and centered 
(along the chamber length) relative to the chamber windows and thus most of the other 
instrumentation. One array is equipped with a single wide -view radiometer with two narrow -
view radiometers that are downstream and two more that are upstream, where all views are 
orthogonal to the chamber axis, as depicted in Figure 4. The n arrow-view radiometers are 
intended to support studies of gas -jet flames, where ACME can accommodate shorter burners, 
making the “lower” detectors useful. The other array, also seen in Fig. 4, provides for three wide-
view measurements of the flame, where one view is masked to nominally block radiant emission 
from the burner. It was specifically designed for the BRE experiment but will be a resource 
available to other ACME experiments. Given that the radiometer array can be exchanged by the 
crew, alternate arrays could be developed.

title: FinalRpt_ACMEFlameDesign
text:
ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 
15 
 
 
 
Figure 4: Crew-exchangeable radiometer arrays on the ACME chamber insert: (top) standard 
(ACME) array of 5 radiometers, and (bottom) array with three radiometers, designed for the BRE 
experiment, where the lowest detector is masked to avoid view of the burner. 
 
A third radiometer array was used in the CFI-G experiment and the second round of the Flame 
Design experiment, where it is important to understand that only a single radiometer array can be 
used at a time. Unlike ACME’s other radiometer arrays, each sensor in the CFI -G array has two 
fixed gains, i.e., a high gain and low gain. It is described in the Cool Flames Radiometer 
Characterization Report (CIR-RPT-4600). 
 
The narrow-view radiometers in the standard array are only fully sensitive in small spots, but they 
are each sensitive in a much greater Field of View (FOV) than represented in the preceding figure. 
They do not have lenses; their FOV is a result of an aperture where most of their FOV is within the 
penumbra which is only visible to a portion of the sensor. Figures representing the measured FOVs

title: FinalRpt_ACMEFlameDesign
text:
ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 
16 
 
 
of the as -built standard and BRE radiometer arrays are found in section 3.F of the ACME 
Engineering Implementation report. 
 
Unfortunately, the radio meters in the BRE array typically saturated in the first round of BRE 
testing, so the standard array was used in its second round. However, those radiometers similarly 
saturated in many of round 2 tests. In this regard, each of ACME’s BRE and standard radiometers 
have a fixed gain. 
 
Radiometers in the standard ACME array regrettably saturated in most of Flame Design’s first 
round of testing so it was replaced with the CFI-G array in the second round. 
 
For more information about the standard radiometer ar ray used for most ACME testing, see the 
Radiometer Characterization Report (ACME-RPT-011). Meanwhile, you can learn about the array 
used in the first round of BRE testing from the BRE Radiometer Characterization Report (ACME -
RPT-012). 
 
An additional wide -view radiometer, that is fixed and not crew exchangeable, is positioned 
downstream of the burner and flame at 30 o from the chamber axis. This detector is primarily 
intended to support the spherical flame experiments and will have a quicker response than the 
more sensitive detectors that will used in the linear arrays. Like the radiometers on the two linear 
arrays, it will have a spectral range of nominally 0.2 -11 micron and its fie ld of view will be 
established by an appropriately selected aperture. 
 
The FOV of the off -set radiometer is also shown in section 3.F of the ACME Engineering 
Implementation report . Learn more about this sensor from the Radiometer Characterization 
Report (ACME-RPT-011). 
 
To detect the quenching of dim flames, the chamber insert will be equipped with a set of three 
PMTs. Each PMT will have a wide-angle view, a sight line that is orthogonal to the chamber axis, 
and will be centered (along the chamber length) relative to the chamber windows so that it is 
aligned with most of the other instrumentation. The PMTs’ spectral range will be 230 -700 nm, 
i.e., visible and near ultraviolet, but one will have a 310-nm bandpass filter and another will have 
a 430-nm bandpass filter (where both are with a 10-nm FWHM). The pair of detectors will enable 
measurement of OH* and CH* emission, respectively. The third PMT will be equipped with a 
neutral density filter to prevent saturation. Like many other components, the PMT array can be 
removed from the chamber insert by the crew. 
 
Unlike the radiometers, each PMT had a readily adjustable gain. However, the PMT signals 
sometimes saturated when the gains were set too high. See the PMT Characterization Report 
(ACME-RPT-013) to learn more about the three Photomultiplier Tube (PMTs). 
 
The chamber insert is also equipped with six far -field thermocouples to measure the spread of 
the thermal field in the spherical flame experiments. They are of limited utility for other 
experiments because they are positioned upstream of the burner tip. Therefore, they will 
generally not be installed by the crew to reduce the chance of accidental damage. There will be 
two versions of a four-thermocouple rake to allow a choice of near and far measurements. Other

title: FinalRpt_ACMEFlameDesign
text:
ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 
17 
 
 
arrays could be designed to support future experiments, but they cannot extend downstream of 
the burner tip without interfering with other (e.g., optical) measurements. 
 
The two lone thermocouples, which are both at nominally 200 mm from the center of the spherical 
burner, were installed throughout ACME testing. The tip of one was seen to be slightly bent early 
in testing, as discussed and depicted in section 3.G of the ACME Engineering Implementa tion 
report. 
 
The short (or far) version of the thermocouple rake was used throughout ACME testing, except for 
the final day of CFI-G testing and first round-two day of Flame Design testing, which both featured 
normal flames, even though second rounds of each study were otherwise with inverse flames . 
Factors which led to the limited use of the short thermocouple rake included the need for crew 
time to switch between rakes and the potential adverse effects, such as heat loss and quenching, 
of the long (close) rake. The short (far) rake’s thermocouple tips should nominally be at 45, 60, 
100, and 100 mm from the spherical burner center. Meanwhile, the thermocouples of the long 
(near) rake should nominally be at 13, 25, 50, and 100 mm from the spherical burner center. 
 
For thermocouples at the same distance from the burner center, the angle between the rays from 
the burner center to the two thermocouples should be 90 degrees. The bead size of the 
thermocouples was not measured, but it is undoubte dly at least twice the size of the 0.2 mm 
diameter wire. 
 
The two thermocouples closest to the burner outlets on each four -thermocouple rake are type B, 
while the others are type K. 
 
Experiment-unique hardware is also mounted on the chamber insert. For example, to 
accommodate the E-FIELD Flames experiment, the insert is equipped with a high -voltage supply 
and a crew-removable electrode mesh which can be set between +10 and -10 kV. The circular mesh 
is orthogonal to the chamber axis and is positioned (during set up) at either ~35 or ~50 mm 
downstream of the insulated burner. The ion current between the burner and electrode mesh will 
be determined via measurement of the voltage drop a cross a known resistor and application of 
Ohm’s Law. 
 
Additional images of the chamber insert can be seen in the ACME Engineering Implementation 
report, where the hardware specific to E -FIELD Flames is discussed further in section 2.B of that 
report. 
 
Additional supporting measurements will be made, where the chamber pressure is a simple 
example. The ACME experiments will use the CIR’s gas chromatograph for pre - and post-test 
analysis of the chamber atmosphere, e.g., for oxygen, nitrogen, carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, 
and fuel gases. Acceleration measurements will be provided by the Space Acceleration 
Measurement System (SAMS) [27], which is the primary instr ument for such measurements on 
ISS and previously served that role for the space shuttle. 
 
The CIR’s Gas Chromatograph Instrumentation Package (GCIP) was not used for the CFI-G, CLD 
Flame, or E-FIELD Flames investigations but was sometimes used during BRE, Flame Design, and 
s-Flame testing. Its use require d significant time and as such effectively reduce d the number of

title: FinalRpt_ACMEFlameDesign
text:
ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 
18 
 
 
tests that c ould be conducted. However, estimates of the chamber contents were computed 
assuming that the fuel in a normal flame test (for example) was either fully or not at all oxidized, 
e.g., for unsustained ignition in the latter case. 
 
The CIR facility was equipped with a 3-axis SAMS sensor head and the acceleration measurements, 
along with relevant documentation, are accessible via the home page for the Principal Investigator 
Microgravity Services (PIMS) , https://gipoc.grc.nasa.gov/wp/pims/home/. To be clear, the 
acceleration measurements are not archived with the ACME experiment data in the Physical 
Sciences Informatics (PSI) website, www.nasa.gov/PSI. 
 
All ACME experiments will be constant volume (i.e., rather than constant pressure) studies, where 
the chamber’s free volume will be about 90 liters. Burner flows will generally be constrained to 
limit the pressure rise, and tests will typically be 0.5-2 minutes in duration. 
 
The chamber’s free volume is approximately 83 liters depending on the installed hardware. 
 
The ACME experiments will be configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew. Instead, the 
experiments will be commanded from the ground, specifically from the Telescience Support 
Center (TSC) at the NASA Glenn Research Center in Cleveland, Ohio. They can be conducted in a 
nominally automated mode using pre -programmed scripts. However, it will also be possible to 
effectively operate the experiments in a “manual” mode, where changes can be made in response 
to the analog video downlink and the numerical data available in the telemetry stream. For 
example, a flow rate could be adjusted to approach a stability or soot limit. Step and ramp 
changes can be made in the flow rate(s) or electric field pot ential. The TFP fiber array can be 
translated uniformly through a soot -free flame to get a continuum measurement of the 
temperature field. In summary, ACME’s experiment control will allow for broad flexibility. 
 
The TSC is now also referred to as the Glenn ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC). ACME tests 
were always conducted in a nominally automated mode. 
 
B. Hardware Shortcomings 
From the Flame Design PI, Rich Axelbaum: 
“The only significant disappointment with the project was with the diagnostics, 
particularly with respect to gas temperature and soot volume fraction. They were not at 
the level that the team would have hoped. Much of this was due to the fact that the 
diagnostics were outdated by the time they were used in our experiments on the ISS, and 
thus the diagnostics and calibrations were not at the level that we expect in a laboratory 
experiment. Of course, the ISS has constraints that limit the ability to incorporate state-
of-the-art diagnostics, and this likely made this weakness unavoidable, but it would have 
been valuable to have had more flexibility in terms of being able to upgrade the 
diagnostics with more modern cameras and instrumentation.” 
 
ACME’s sintered spherical burners did not always yield spherically symmetric flames which are 
centered on the burner’s center, where that combination is important for true spherical 
symmetry. While nominally spherical at moderate flow rates, the flame’s center bec ame 
increasing offset from the burner center as the flow rate was increased. It is very likely that the 
sintered attachment of the sphere to the supply tube is more porous than the sintered sphere

itself because the flame is seen to be shifted toward the supp ly tube. There was significant 
improvement when the starting burner (serial number 1002) was replaced mid -way through 
round 1 with an alternate burner (serial number 1003), which continued to be used for spherical 
flame testing throughout the remainder of ACME operations. Nonetheless, the symmetry was 
not perfect, which is a shortcoming of the Flame Design data. 
 
On 27 Dec. 2021 (GMT 361), it was determined that the Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP) fiber array 
was not aligned to the ACME Data Camera (DataCam ) as intended, i.e., so that the fibers would 
be orthogonal relative to the camera. Unfortunately, this was the fourth day of testing in which 
the fiber array wasn’t aligned, where it regrettably wasn’t recognized earlier. Given the 
importance of the TFP-derived measurements of the flame temperature, testing was halted until 
the array was aligned (with other crew tasks) by astronaut Raja Chari on 17 Jan. 2022 (GMT 017). 
 
The signal from the standard ACME radiometer array used in round 1 of Flame Design testing was 
saturated for nearly every test, yielding non -useful data. For round 2, that sensor array was 
replaced with the one designed for Cool Flames Investigation with Gases (CFI -G) which yielded 
satisfactory measurements. 
 
ACME’s Mass Flow Controllers (MFCs) used to control the flow of fuel, nitrogen, and oxidizer did 
not always perform adequately, where the flow rates were not always appropriately steady or at 
the intended value. However, the resulting effects on the flame behavior are tentatively assumed 
to be minor. 
 
In addition to sections 3.A-B, shortcomings are discussed in Appendices B and C of this report and 
in the ACME Engineering Implementation document. The latter document includes discussion of 
deviations and waivers (in section 4.B), etc. 
 
 
4. Preliminary Results 
A. Changed Test Plans 
A change was made to the CIR combustion chamber’s pressure limit on 17 Jan. 2022 (by astronaut 
Raja Chari) to enable Flame Design testing at chamber pressures of up to 3 atm in the final round-
2 test days, whereas the limit had been 1.5 atm in preceding testing. In his request for this change, 
Flame Design PI Rich Axelbaum explained: 
“One of the fundamental goals of Flame Design is to achieve sooting limits. We are unsure 
if we will be able to attain a range of sooting flames with the current ambient fuel 
constraints. One way to increase soot formation, and thus the range of the test matrix, 
is via higher pressures, so this capability can help to ensure we me et our science goals. 
Another fundamental goal of Flame Design is to understand flame extinction. Our recent 
analysis suggests that pressure is a critical variable when predicting flame extinction, and 
in can influence flame chemistry in ways that we had not anticipated. Obtaining 
extinction data over a wide range of pressures could also be valuable for spacecraft fire 
safety.” 
 
An additional normal-flames test day was added to the start of the second round of testing (even 
though that was focused on inverse flames) to acquire data useful for calibrating the Thin Filament 
Pyrometry (TFP) measurements. With that goal, the added test day, conducted on 28 Oct. 2021

text:
ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 
20 
 
 
(GMT 301), was carried out with the long (near) thermocouple rake, where all other Flame Design 
tests were conducted with the short (far) rake. In his request for this additional test day, the PI 
stated in part: 
“The ability to validate the TFP is very important for most of the ACME experiments. Thus, 
measuring the near-field temperatures under conditions where we have TFP data would 
be highly desirable, almost required. … These results would be the only measurem ents 
ACME has with a direct comparison with TFP, and since we already know exactly which 
flames to run to get good data, we know that we will be successful in obtaining this data 
and validating the TFP data. … Reiterating, this extra day would directly benefit all of the 
temperature data of Flame Design, and all of the spherical flame ACME experiments, by 
providing at least one direct validation of the TFP method. As you know, we have 
uncertainties about the accuracy of the TFP technique we are using in the ACME rig, and 
having these T/C measurements could have a profound impact on the ACME results.” 
 
As discussed in the previous section, the decision was made to use the CFI-G radiometer array in 
Flame Design’s second round of testing rather than the standard ACME array that often saturated 
in the earlier testing. 
 
Coiled igniter tips were also used in the second round of testing instead of the loop igniter tips 
used in the first round, where the coiled were believed to be more robust. 
 
Other changes to the test plans were minor in comparison. 
 
B. Overview of Experiment Test Operations 
While not yet prepared, additional details will be made available in the ACME/ Flame Design 
Experimental Procedure document. 
 
The narrative description of the experimental procedure is an excerpt from the ‘Methods / 
Experimental’ section of the following conference paper. 
Y.-C. Chien, J. Tinajero, D. Stocker, U. Hegde, and D. Dunn -Rankin, “Electric Field Effects on 
Flames in Microgravity on the International Space Station,” 2018 Spring Technical Meeting of 
the Central States Section of The Combustion Institute, Minneapolis, MN, 20-22 May 2018. 
 
While the paper was written for the Electric -Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E -FIELD 
Flames) experiment, much of the discussion applies to ACME in general, including the Flame 
Design investigation. The figure referenced in this excerpt is not i ncluded herein. Clarifications 
and additional information, not in the conference paper, are included in boxed notes like this. 
 
The CIR experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew. Thus far, ACME’s activity 
has included the majority of the crew members, regardless of their nationalities. Most often the 
astronauts and cosmonauts exchange gas bottles, mass flow controllers, and igniter tips. In the 
latter case, the igniter tip exchange can occur after failure or proactively before failure when the 
crew already has changes to make changes in the interior of the insert. While these activities may 
seem mundane, the crew play a critical role in setting up the hardware for each experiment. As 
an extreme example, there were crew activities on 8 separate days in Sept.-Oct. 2017 to configure 
the CIR and ACME hardware for the first ACME experiment, namely the Coflow Laminar Diffusion 
Flame (CLD Flame) experiment. In contrast, only two crew days were required to reconfigure the

title: FinalRpt_ACMEFlameDesign
text:
ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 
21 
 
 
hardware for the first E-FIELD Flames tests because of the initial use of the same coflow burner. 
Planning is critical because crew activity is scheduled three weeks in advance, for which detailed 
procedures must be prepared and uplinked to the ISS. 
 
As a correction, including two maintenance activities, there were 11 crew days in Sept.-Oct. 2017 
to prepare for the initial CLD Flame testing on the space station. 
 
All CIR tests are remotely commanded from the ground from NASA’s Glenn ISS Payload Operations 
Center (GIPOC) in Cleveland, Ohio. Typically , four to six people staff four consoles during the 
testing. The CIR hardware is controlled from the Rack Officer (RO) and Data Management Officer 
(DMO) consoles, and the ACME hardware is controlled from the Payload Developer (PD) console. 
Two shifts of personnel are scheduled to staff these three consoles on test days because they 
typically last 14 hours with the many pre - and post-testing activities. Given that the tests are 
remotely commanded, the operations are carried out in the day and evening in Cleveland, e.g., 
from 7 AM to 9 PM. A day’s tests, i.e., with flames, are normally conducted in a period of 10 hours 
of less. Tests are normally conducted on three weekdays per two weeks. On intervening 
weekdays, the image dat a is downlinked and the crew often swap one or both gas bottles. 
Transferring and downlinking data from a day’s tests also requires a 2 -shift day for the RO and 
DMO consoles, where it is always necessary to verify that data was downlinked without errors 
and that data is not missing. Those two positions are also staffed to guide and oversee the crew 
activity. As a result, the CIR consoles are normally actively staffed on four weekdays per week. A 
team of four carry out the detailed planning for the CIR a nd ACME console staff, and the daily 
operational plans typically exceed 50 pages on days including testing. 
 
The science console allows for review of the analog video and non-imaging telemetry (at 1 Hz) in 
near real time but doesn’t allow for commanding. In the case of E -FIELD Flames, arrangements 
were made so that the analog video is streamed to a secure computer at UC Irvine to allow the 
research team to participate in test operations and to recommend adjustments to the day’s 
planned parameters. That te am does not see the telemetry during the testing, but is in 
communication via phone and e -mail with their NASA research partners at the GRC ISS Payload 
Operations Center (GIPOC). While there are many preparatory steps, the tests are ultimately 
conducted using an uploaded software script and parameter files. In advance of the test day, the 
UC Irvine science team plans the nearly 60 parameters in the voltage sweep script and specifies 
other parameters that are configured outside of the script, such as camer a settings. It is also 
possible to effectively conduct tests in a ‘manual’ mode, where parameters are changed in 
response to the analog video downlink or telemetry. For example, the electric field potential can 
be adjusted to approach a stability or soot limit. 
 
Provisions were made to enable the investigators from all ACME experiments to remotely view the 
analog video while they communicated verbally with NASA science personnel in the operations 
center. All ACME flame tests, including those for Flame Design, were conducted in a nominally 
automated manner using software scripts and extensive parameter files. 
 
Typically, ten E-FIELD Flames tests are conducted per test day. Despite the short test durations, 
the low rate results from several unavoidable factors. After a test is conducted, the 125-Hz non-
imaging data is downlinked for immediate review by the science team. A small sample of images 
are often downlinked to ensure that the camera exposures are appropriate, where the times for

title: FinalRpt_ACMEFlameDesign
text:
ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 
22 
 
 
those images are typically selected based on non-imaging data to provide extreme examples. The 
review helps to verify parameters or plan for adjustments in subsequent tests, e.g., to select the 
voltage range after determining where the ion current saturates for the given fl ame conditions. 
After a test is conducted, a fan circulates the chamber atmosphere after which the chamber is 
vented (to space) back to atmospheric pressure, if needed. Midway through a day’s E -FIELD 
Flames tests, the atmosphere is circulated for 15 minu tes through a filter cartridge filled with 
molecular sieves to capture any soot and adsorb at least a portion of the combustion products, 
e.g., carbon dioxide, water vapor, and incomplete combustion products. The tests are only 
conducted when both Ku and S band communication is available through NASA’s Tracking and 
Data Relay Satellite (TDRS) System. Depending on the various orbits, there are periodic 
communication outages with a loss of signal (LOS) that can be a short handover (from one satellite 
to another) or can last as long as 30 minutes. 
 
An average of 16 tests were conducted per Flame Design test day, where ignition was typically 
unsuccessful (e.g., un-sustained) in a couple of tests. 
 
In contrast to E-FIELD Flames, recirculation during Flame Design inverse-flame test operations was 
only conducted prior to venting at the end of a test day. During normal -flame testing, it was 
usually conducted once in the midst of testing, as done with E-FIELD Flames. Exceptions were test 
days 19115, 19123, and 19137 (the first three days with flames); 19161 (when no flames were 
ignited); 19206 (the last test day in the first round of testing), and 21301 (the first day of the second 
round of testing). Another exception was on 19150 when it was carried out duri ng the midst of 
testing and then again when the combustion chamber was vented and refilled for additional tests 
on the same day. 
 
A variety of constraints limit the number of tests that can be performed, both overall and on a 
daily basis. The next combustion experiments in the CIR will feature solid fuels and focus on flame 
spread and material flammability. That follow -on plan limits the duration of ACME operations, 
where each ACME experiment is allotted four months for testing. Although it requires additional 
crew time, these allotments are split into two rounds so that the investigators have a break from 
testing for careful review of the early results so that they can maximize the scientific outcome of 
their second round. This paper reports on early results from the first round of E-FIELD Flames. 
 
While nitrogen is available from the space station, the combustion testing is limited by the 
available gas bottles that were and are launched to support the tests. For E -FIELD Flames and 
most of ACME’s experiments, the test matrices used to plan those gas resources were established 
in 2010. At that time, NASA limited the scope of the ACME tests matrices with the intent of 
focused experiments with limited objectives rather than comprehensive experiments. As s uch, 
the general target was 50 tests per experiment. For most ACME experiments, the limiting gas 
constraint is the oxygen/nitrogen bottles used to fill the chamber. This resource constraint is 
exacerbated by the CIR because it is equipped with a pair of redundant safety timers to limit the 
fuel that can flow into the combustion chamber (where the timers can be set for the oxidizer flow 
in the case of inverse flame testing). The timers can only be reset by venting the combustion 
chamber. Therefore, the timer limit combined with other constraints effectively corresponds to 
the day’s maximum flow time for the fuel (or more generally, the limiting reactant). For E -FIELD 
Flames, the safety timers are set to the maximum value of 999 seconds, which corresponds to the 
10 tests typically completed per day.

The maximum limit of 999 seconds for the valve safety timers was used for all ACME testing. 
 
Another constraint is the available time in a day, where the console personnel and ISS resources, 
such as the video downlink, are planned for a limited number of hours. When necessary for the 
research, NASA does have continuous 24 -hour/day operations for some non -CIR experiments. 
But as discussed, the ACME tests are typically two minutes or less in duration, so the testing is 
almost always limited to the planned durations. 
 
Data limits are yet another constraint, where the on -orbit hardware can store a limited amount 
of data. More importantly, 127,000 MB is the most that can be reasonably managed in a two -
shift transfer and downlink day. Therefore, tests days are limited to this amount of data, where 
image data from select cameras is often archived at reduced rates to mitigate this challenge. 
Nonetheless, the limit sometimes forces decisions to abandon recorded images. 
 
This detailed description of operations and hardware provides the context under which the ACME 
experiments are conducted. …
