title: s_Flame_final_report_20210729
text:
ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 29 July 2021 
61 
 
Pre-flight and post-flight activities are generally not addressed in this report. 
 
B. List of Preflight, In-flight, Postflight Anomalies 
1. Mission anomalies 
While there were certainly issues with testing discussed in the next section, there 
were no significant anomalies during s -Flame’s Increment 63 testing. However, 
anomalies did occur during Increment 60 and 61 which led to corrective actions 
and/or make-up testing. 
 
2. Any other difficulties in obtaining scientific data 
Ignition of the flames presented a significant challenge to the experiment during this 
increment. All of the flame tests were conducted where the fuel and chamber 
atmosphere were both diluted with helium rather than the nitrogen used in 
Increments 60 and 61. The two gases’ properties are dramatically different making 
comparison testing very desirable for manifestation of different phenomena. 
Helium’s thermal conductivity is notably several times greater than that of nitrogen, 
so considerably more energy and power was required to ignite the flames. The power 
level was slowly increased from test to test until ignition was finally achieved on the 
ninth test, where only seven flames were ignited of the 15 tests conducted on May 11 
(20132), the first day for fla mes in Increment 63. The cautious approach was taken 
because of concerns that the igniter tip might fail (i.e., burn out) if too much power 
was applied. An igniter failure would have likely halted testing for weeks given the 
need to schedule the commander’s time to replace the igniter tip. 
 
After that first test day, the decision was made to have the igniter replaced with a coil 
rather than loop design which was believed to be more robust because of the thicker 
wire. Furthermore, the igniter tip had not been replaced in months, and the tips do 
degrade with time, especially when they are not quickly retracted from the ignited 
flames. The coil igniter was used successfully but still with caution, where flames were 
not always ignited successfully. Subseque ntly, some tests were conducted in 
atmosphere with ~30% oxygen (by volume) instead of the planned ~21%. As one 
would expect, that proved to be helpful for achieving ignition. But the end result was 
that some tests were conducted with 21% oxygen, some at 30%, and some at both 
nominal concentrations. Fortuitously, this mixture of conditions may provide deeper 
insight into the mechanisms of flame dynamics and response. 
 
Tests are also unsuccessful when the flame fails to ignite, where that occurred, for 
example, during Increment 61 in tests 19304A4, 19304A6, 19308C1, and 20006A1. 
That can be corrected by adjusting various test parameters and other settings. In this 
case, adjustments were subsequently made to the ignition position (e.g., after 
19304A4 and 19304A6), the relative timing of the fuel flow and igniter activation (e.g., 
after 19308C1), and the duration of the igniter activation (e.g., after 20006A1). As 
another example, failed ignition can result from false ignition detection and

title: s_Flame_final_report_20210729
text:
ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 29 July 2021 
62 
 
deactivation re sulting from the combination of settings for ignition and detection, 
e.g., the gain for the Photomultiplier Tube (PMT) module measuring the OH* 
chemiluminescence. The latter, in the ultraviolet at 310 nm, is a good indicator of an 
ignited flame rather than the glowing igniter, which emits primarily in the infrared and 
visible spectrum. 
 
Testing on June 3 (20155) was cut short due to a combination of issues. The final test 
was aborted due to an error with an Image Processing and Storage Unit (IPSU). 
Consoles needed to be reset for the new increment, and there was an issue with the 
Fuel Oxidizer Management Assembly (FOMA) Control Unit, i.e. the FCU. Rebooting 
the FCU ina dvertently set the valve safety timers to zero, which cannot be reset 
without venting and refilling the combustion chamber with the intended atmosphere. 
Those issues combined with an extended loss of commanding prevented further 
science operations on that day. Therefore, an additional test day (July 8, i.e., 20190) 
was added to make up for lost science, e.g., where only one test was successfully 
conducted at ~21% oxygen on June 3. The FCU was off nominal because of a high 
carrier gas pressure in the Gas Chromatograph Instrumentation Package (GCIP). 
Imaging of the hydrogen flames was often an issue, where they were not apparent or hardly 
visible to the operations camera and ACME DataCam, where the latter is the primary camera 
for ACME testing. The testi ng with the extremely dim flames was limited to that conducted 
on Dec. 18 (19352), Jan. 24 (20024), June 3 (20155), and July 8 (20190). This shortcoming 
unfortunately inhibits assessment of the three -dimensional flame symmetry as the two 
intensified cameras were opposite of each other. 
 
The flow ranges of the selected Mass Flow Controllers (MFCs) was found to be a 
challenge, where it was discovered that the goal of studying both kinetic and radiative 
extinction was not always satisfactorily achieved because of flow rate constraints. 
 
At high flow rates, the burner does not produce spherically symmetric flames. While 
nominally spherical at moderate flow rates, the flame’s center becomes increasing 
offset from the burner center. More specifically, the flam e is shifted toward the 
supply tube indicating that the sintered attachment of the poro us sphere to the 
supply tube is more ‘open’ than the pores of the spherical burner. In other words, the 
flow from the burner is not spherically symmetric. At sufficiently high flow rates, the 
flame becomes obviously non-spherical, where it can appear to be ellipsoidal or even 
parabolic in shape. In the latter case, the flame locally quenches near the supply tube. 
 
When at a small fraction of the maximum flow rate, Mass Flow Controller (MFC) 
performance has been seen to be poor during s-Flame testing, i.e., where actual flow 
rate differed from that desired. However, this was not a surprise to those familiar 
with the hardware. 
 
Flow perturbations have been noticed in som e s-Flame tests, where ACME’s MFCs 
used to control the flow of fuel, nitrogen, and oxidizer have unfortunately not always

title: s_Flame_final_report_20210729
text:
ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 29 July 2021 
63 
 
performed satisfactorily. In tests conducted using the 1 -slpm fuel MFC (where the 
flow range is on a nitrogen basis), the flow has be en seen to overshoot and 
undershoot when first opening. Small flow irregularities have been most apparent 
through their effect on the Photomultiplier Tube (PMT) measurements, e.g., of OH* 
and CH* chemiluminescence. A momentary increase in fuel flow, as h as occurred in 
some s-Flame tests, naturally leads to increased light from the flame. T he MFCs are 
tested - without flames - after they are first installed. Adjustments are typically made 
to (1) the setting that controls when the valves open and (2) the Proportional-Integral-
Derivative (PID) settings. This ACME activity has involved signif icant testing, where 
there is an assortment of MFCs with different flow ranges for each of the three gas 
types. While the MFC adjustments have been beneficial, they have not eliminated all 
gas flow problems. It was seen in prior ACME testing that nitrogen oscillations (if any) 
tend to damp with time, so a nitrogen pre -flow can be used so that such oscillations 
might end before the flame is ignited. As another measure, the MFCs are re-zeroed 
prior to each test, where that was another measure adopted in earlier ACME testing. 
 
As mentioned previously, s -Flame tests have sometimes automatically aborted 
(because of the controlling software script), where that is normally pri or to gas flow 
and the activation of the igniter – which is typical for other ACME expe riments. As a 
result, there was little lost other than the available experimental time in the failed test 
attempt. ACME aborts normally occur because of communication issues with an IPSU, 
which for example happened for tests 19304A5, 19352D3, 19352P1, 20 024N1, and 
20024J1. A few other tests aborted because flow rates were accidentally specified 
outside of the range of the installed mass flow controller(s), where that included for 
example 19352A1, 19352D2, and 20013C2. ACME aborts are infrequent, but th ere 
are sometimes days when they occur repeatedly as can be seen here. 
 
C. Completeness/Quality of Data 
During Increments 60 and 61, nine days of tests were conducted during which 145 flames 
were ignited for the first round of testing. In contrast, only 29 tests were specified as 
required or highly desired in the ACME Integrated Science Requirements Document 
(ISRD) for that round. Therefore, a wealth of data was obtained for this round of testing 
which featured gaseous fuels diluted by nitrogen. 
 
However, t here was a significant loss of data. Most importantly, the first fuel bottle 
appeared to leak on installation (in Increment 60) and later on-orbit testing (in Increment 
61) with other hydrogen/methane blends suggests that its fuel mixture would have been 
ideal for achieving science success. Furthermore, there was significant image data loss 
on two different test days, specifically Sept. 13 (19256) and Dec. 18 (19352). As a result, 
those test days were nominally repeated on Jan. 29 (20029) and Jan. 24 (20 024), 
respectively (i.e., in a reversed order). For these reasons, a simple comparison of the total 
number of flames ignited (145) with that specified as required or hi ghly desired (29) for 
the first round of testing is somewhat misleading.

title: s_Flame_final_report_20210729
text:
ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 29 July 2021 
64 
 
As discussed in the preceding section, the hydrogen and diluted -hydrogen flames were 
not apparent or extremely dim in imaging from the operations camera and ACME 
DataCam. Neglecting that factor, the cameras are sensitive to radiation where pixels 
gradually become ‘hot’ (i.e., dead) over time. While these bright spots are addressed in 
image post-processing, they are a degradation of the image quality. 
 
It is possible that the tests are subtly affected by the acceleration environment, but there 
is not obvious indication of this; and it has thus far not been evaluated with available 
measurements from the Space Acceleration Measurement System (SAMS). 
 
D. Status of Data Analysis [provided by Prof. Stephen Tse, Rutgers U.] 
Image files are currently being processed. Radial pos itions of maximum CH* 
chemiluminescence is being plotted against time. Different radii are being considered 
and plotted together, as some flames are not completely symmetric. MFC and PMT data 
are being compared with video images to assess and confirm exp erimental settings. 
Radiometer data is being reviewed. Analyses of the fiber pyrometry data are ongoing. 
MATLAB code is used to isolate fiber images, which are then color assessed for 
temperature. 
 
Computational simulations with detailed chemistry and tr ansport of the test cases are 
underway. Time -dependent simulations will be compared with the time -dependent 
experimental data, where tracking of the flamefr ont location is based on 
chemiluminescent emission. Steady -state simulations will produce the Isol a curves 
mapping flame response versus system Damkh öler number for given fuel mixtures. The 
experimental cases will then be pin -pointed on the computational mappings to assess 
whether the experimental conditions are in quasi -steady state or near extinctio n limits, 
either kinetic or radiative. Oscillation behavior will be correlated to possib le pulsating 
oscillations found in the simulations. 
 
E. Preliminary Research Findings [provided by Prof. Tse and lightly edited by Stocker] 
The s -Flame experiment utilize s spherically -symmetric diffusion flames and their 
dynamics and responses to investigate fundamental processes, such as extinction, 
instability, and soot formation. 
 
The tests conducted on 19254 (near the end of Increment 60) revealed that a quasi-steady 
flame could be attained for extended duration at low flow rate, i.e., 3 cc/s for 20% 
C2H4/80% N 2 (on a volume basis). The flame was shut down by the automated system 
because the burner reached a cut -off temperature of 250°C. Although the flame 
oscillated near the end of the test, it was likely due to influence of the burner tube. 
Comparisons with computation simulations will help to clarify the involved processes. For 
higher flow rates, e.g., 5 -10 cc/s, with the same mixture, radiative extinctions were 
observed. Generally, the flames showed unstable behavior near the burner tube prior to 
extinction, likely because of lack of fuel mixture and heat loss in that region. Other

title: s_Flame_final_report_20210729
text:
ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 29 July 2021 
65 
 
mixtures, e.g., 25% C2H4/75% N2 and 30% C2H4/70% N2, also showed radiative extinctions 
at higher flow rates. For some cases, the pyrometry fiber interacted with the flam e, 
allowing determination of temperature in on -going analyses. Soot was observed only 
during ignition, which went away as the flame established itself. To assess whether these 
nitrogen-diluted ethylene flames are non-sooty or sooty, cases were run where mixtures 
were ignited and established at low flow rates (e.g., 3 cc/s) with low ethylene contents 
(e.g., 25 -30% C 2H4) and then ramped to high flow rates (e.g., 5 -10 cc /s) with higher 
ethylene contents (e.g., 40 -50% C 2H4). The flames all radiatively exting uished, but no 
sooting was observed. Observations of such radiative extinction behavior at high flow 
rates is an achievement because such phenomenon was not observed in our ground -
based studies, given the limited microgravity durations. Radiative reabsor ption extends 
flame size at extinction. In ISS testing, radiative extinction has been found to be a 
common event, which was predicted computationally, but not observe d previously for 
our flame conditions. 
 
The 19256 tests (in Increment 60) were aimed at examining kinetic extinction. Similar to 
the radiative extinction cases, sufficient microgravity duration is needed to observe 
kinetic extinction because a near steady flame needs to be established first, before ramp 
down in flow rate to find properly the chemical kinetic extinction limit. High flow rate 
cases (e.g., 13.5 cc/s, 15 cc/s) showed asymmetrical flames which radiatively 
extinguished. Flow rates were lowered so that quasi-steady flames could be established 
before ramp down in flow rate. The 15% C2H4 mixtures were not strong enough to sustain 
a quasi-steady flame at 3 cc/s before ramp down. However, for stronger mixtures, i.e., 
20-30% C 2H4, very nice flames were established at 3 cc/s; and kinetic extinctions were 
observed during ramp down before reaching 1 cc/s. Radiative extinctions for ramp up 
cases were also examined. Similarly, for stronger mixtures, i.e., 20 -30% C2H4, very nice 
flames were established at 3 cc/s; and radiative extinctions were observed during ramp 
up before reaching 8 cc/s. 
 
Testing on 19304 investigated 45% CH 4/55% N2 mixtures issuing into an air atmosphere. 
The results indicated that the flow rates specified by the fuel MFC (0.5 slpm) were in the 
regime of kinetic extinction. Quasi-steady flames could not be established. Furthermore, 
larger flow rates could not be provided by the MFC, so observations of radiative extinction 
could not be achieved. Even with a larger capacity MFC, cha racteristically larger flames 
would be expected to be asymmetric. As such, nitroge n-diluted methane flames were 
planned to be reexamined in increased oxygen atmosphere, i.e., 30% O2/70% N2. 
 
Consequently, the 19308 tests investigated nitrogen -diluted meth ane flames in 30% 
O2/70% N2 atmosphere. Various methane concentrations from 45% do wn to 15% were 
examined. For 45% CH 4/55% N2, relatively long duration flames of ~15 s and ~10 s were 
established at flow rates of 2 cc/s and 3 cc/s, respectively. At large r flow rates of 5 and 
9.4 cc/s, the flames expanded to large radii and then extingu ished. These flames 
appeared to demonstrate radiative extinction. Reduction of flow rate from 2 cc/s to 1 
cc/s resulted in extinction during ramp down, indicating kinetic extinction. For 30%

title: s_Flame_final_report_20210729
text:
ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 29 July 2021 
66 
 
CH4/70% N2, flow rates of 3, 5, and 10 cc/s produced flames th at expanded to extinction 
(assumed radiatively); while reduction of flow rate from 3 to 1 cc/s resulted in presumably 
kinetic extinction during ramp down. For 25% CH 4/75% N2, flow rates of 5 and 10 cc/s 
yielded flames that expanded to extinction. For 20% CH4/80% N2, constant flow rate of 
10 cc/s created a flame that expanded until extinction (assumed radiatively); while 
reduction of flow rate from 10 cc/s to 1 cc/s resulted in wavering extinction during ramp 
down, suggesting kinetic extinction. For 15% C H4/85% N 2, flames were ignited, but 
extinguished very quickly. These tests of 19308 suggest that they could manifest both 
radiative and kinetic extinction for the conditions specified. 
 
The 19352 tests examined various concentrations of H2 (45%-70%) diluted with N2 issuing 
into air. The installed fuel MFC had a maximum output of 0.1 slpm, which unfortunately 
provided a less-than-sufficient flow range where its use may have precluded the study of 
radiative extinction corresponding to larger flame sizes. Imaging the diluted hydrogen 
flames was a challenge, especially since the hobj image files from the ACME DataCam 
were mis-formatted. Furthermore, little could be seen in the analog ops imaging, e.g., 
where it, like the DataCam and Cool Flames Investigation (CFI) intensified camera, cannot 
image the ultraviolet OH* flame emission (at 310 nm). Analysis of images from the Low 
Light Level Ultraviolet (LLL -UV) camera and its OH* filter is ongoing. And as one might 
expect, little could be seen with the CFI intensified camera using its broadband CH2O filter. 
Quasi-steady flames seem to be present at low flow rates (e.g., 2.4 cc/s for 70% H 2), as 
inferred from PMT, pyrometry fiber emission, and burner temperature observations. 
Kinetic extinction seems to occur a s the flow rate is ramped down. There were various 
problems with the IPSU and some tests aborted. Using the 100% H 2 bottle with a higher 
flow rate MFC was later performed for tests of 20024 (see below), which was a make-up 
test day added because of the mis-formatting of the DataCam image files. 
 
The tests conducted on 20006, using the 44.4% H 2/55.6% CH 4 bottle, examined 20% 
H2/25% CH 4/55% N 2 mixtures issuing into air. Flam es extinguished, some with wavy 
oscillating behavior prior to extinction. However, it seems that even for very small flow 
rates, e.g., 2 cc/s, extinction was by the radiative mechanism during flame 
expansion. There was too little parameter room in terms of flow rate and burner size to 
identify conclusively kinetic extinction during ram p down for these mixtures. In short, 
radiative extinction (with local flame extinction and re -ignition seemed to occur prior to 
ultimate extinguishment) during flame expansion after ignition was observed. However, 
it is unclear whether ramping down the flow rate resulted in kinetic extinction. Detailed 
analyses of the data are needed. The various cameras seemed to capture the tests well. 
 
The 20013 tests, which used the 6 6.7% H 2/33.3% CH 4 bottle, mainly investigated 30% 
H2/15% CH4/55% N2 mixtures issuing into air. Radiative extinction was difficult to identify 
conclusively because flames with larger flow rates, e.g. 15 cc/s, seemed to last, although 
with patchy extinction areas, until tim e out. Larger flow rates could not be examined 
either because of limited MFC range or distorted flame shape cause by burner limitations 
at high flow rates. Also, kinetic extinction during ramp down could not be identified

title: s_Flame_final_report_20210729
text:
ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 29 July 2021 
67 
 
conclusively, a s some flames see med to extinguish because they were "going into the 
burner." 
 
The 20024 tests using the 100% H 2 bottle repeated and augmented conditions for those 
of 19352 where the 0.1-slpm fuel MFC range was too low to examine radiative extinction 
and the analog and int ensified cameras did not pick up the flame images at all or well. 
Here, the 0.5-slpm fuel MFC was used and only a fused silica filter was used for the Cool 
Flames Investigation (CFI) intensified camera. 45% -15% H 2/N2 balance mixtures wer e 
investigated. The flames at high flow rates, e.g., 10 cc/s, did not extinguish, appearing 
quasi-steady until time out. The pyrometry fibers glowed, perhaps making good flame -
structure measurements, which will be evaluated subsequently. The flames seem ed to 
extinguish during ramp down, but further analysis is needed to assess kinetic extinction. 
 
The tests conducted on 20029 used 50% C 2H4/50% N 2 and repeated and augmented 
conditions of 19256, when the images were not good. Again, the results indicated both 
kinetic and radiative extinction phenomena under corresponding conditions. However, 
no sooting flames were established, necessitating 100% C 2H4 and an enriched oxygen 
atmosphere to facilitate sooting behavior in possible future tests. 
 
The 20132 test s kicked off a round of tests with helium -diluted fuel and oxidizer. The 
ambient was 21% O2 and 79% He. The fuel was composed of 25% H 2, 20% CH4, and 55% 
He. Using He as inert made igniting the mixture much more difficult compared to that for 
the N2 inert cases of Round 1, using the same ignition parameters. The reason is believed 
to be due to the 6X higher value in thermal conductivity of He versus that of N 2. As a 
result, ignition parameters were varied, e.g., with a longer preheat time and higher 
power, to achieve ignition for the He-diluted mixtures and ambient. The tests produced 
flames at 3, 5, 7, and 10 cc/s that expanded outwardly quickly and extinguished. For 5, 7, 
and 10 cc/s, the flames seemed to disappear and 're -ignite' with a "flash" bef ore final 
extinction. We are currently investigating the flash phenomenon. Moreover, the 
radiation mechanism is not conclusive, as it appears different than for the N 2-diluted 
cases. We did not have a chance to examine lowering of flow rates to assess kinetic 
extinction. 
 
The 20136 tests examined 20% H 2/25% CH4/55% He issuing into 21% O 2/He. For 5 cc/s 
and 7 cc/s, the mixture ignites but immediately extinguishes, with almost no observable 
flame-front expansion. For 10, 13, 15, and 17.5 cc/s, the mixtures ignite, expand quickly, 
and extinguish. We believe that the extinction mechanism is radiative and will compare 
with computational simulations. For the cases with a ramp down in flow rate, the flames 
seemed to extinguish before ramp down. Thus, we were not able to assess purely kinetic 
extinction. Ignition parameters were varied to investigate thresholds for igniting the 
mixture for different flow rates. Only flow rates above 7 cc/s showed flame -front 
expansion leading to extinction, with 17.5 cc/s showing a flash or wavering of the flame 
before final extinction.

title: s_Flame_final_report_20210729
text:
ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 29 July 2021 
68 
 
The tests conducted on 20142 investigated 30% H 2/15% CH 4/55% He issuing into 30% 
O2/He. Elevated oxygen was approved for study, since ignition and extinction limits in 
previous testing were affected by t he high thermal conductivity of He. For 5, 7, 10, 15, 
13, and 16.5 cc/s flow rates, nice flames were established that expanded to 
wavy/oscillating extinction at the end, indicative of radiative extinction. For the cases 
with a ramp down in flow rate, the flames seemed to extinguish during the ignition flow 
rate stage before ramp down. Thus, we were not able to assess kinetic extinction. 
 
The 20155 tests examined 45% H 2/55% He issuing into 30% O 2/He and 21% O 2/He. 
Previous tests using He as inert had shown that much larger energy and power are needed 
to ignite the mixtures. For the 30% O 2/H2 atmosphere, the tests produced flames at 10 
and 14 cc/s (MFC limit of 1 SLMP) that expanded after ignition, but were extinguished by 
the automated protocol because the burner reached the 250°C temperature limit before 
any self-extinction could occur. The flames were not too large at the end. Presumably, 
the thermally-conductive He diluent facilitates heat transfer to the burner. For the cases 
with a ramp down in fl ow rate, i.e., starting at 10 and 14 cc/s and ramping down, the 
flames seemed to self-extinguish during ramp down. Flow rate at 5 cc/s results in flames 
that only existed briefly. Extinction at this lower flow rate is probably due to heat loss to 
the burner, rather than pure kinetic extinction. Ramp down from 14 cc/s towards 5 cc/s 
resulted in the burner reaching the 250 °C limit during ramp down. More analyses are 
needed. Tests at 21% O 2/He atmosphere were limited. Fuel flow of 5 cc/s s howed flash 
ignition, but no sustained flame. Meanwhile, 10 cc/s resulted in a flame that seemed to 
expand to self-extinction. 
 
Testing on 20160 investigated 45% CH 4/55% He issuing into 30% O 2/He and 21% O 2/He. 
Without H 2 in the mixture, even larger ener gy and power we re needed to ignite the 
mixtures. For the 30% O 2/H2 atmosphere, the 5, 10, and 15 cc/s flow rates were sooty 
only at ignition; and the subsequent non -sooty flames expanded to self -extinction. At 3 
and 4 cc/s, the mixtures flashed at ignition, and extinguished almost immediately. It was 
not clear whether extinction was due to kinetic extinction or heat loss to the burner. At 
6 and 7 cc/s, flames ignited with less soot, expanding with no soot to self-extinction. The 
case with a ramp down i n flow rate cou ld not conclusively identify kinetic extinction. 
More analysis is needed. Tests at 21% O2/He atmosphere needed even more energy and 
power for ignition. At 5, 7, 10, and 15 cc/s, flames ignited with soot, and expanded quickly 
to extinction. 
 
The 20164 tests began study of ethylene -based flames, where 20% C 2H4/80% He issued 
into 30% O 2/He and 21% O 2/He atmospheres. For 5 cc/s, the flame expanded and 
remained quasi-steady until the burner limit temperature (250°C) was reached. At 6, 7, 
10, and 15 cc/s, the flames expanded to extinction, with the higher flow rates (i.e., 10 and 
15 cc/s) exhibiting sooty ignition. Fuel flow of 5.5 cc/s seemed to correspond to a 
condition where the onset of oscillating extinction was simultaneous with the burn er 
reaching the 250°C temperature limit. For the cases with a ramp down in flow rate, the 
flames seemed to extinguish during ramp down, but heat loss to the burner may be the

title: s_Flame_final_report_20210729
text:
ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 29 July 2021 
69 
 
mechanism of extinction. Although 13 tests were conducted with the 21% O2/He 
atmosphere, ignition was not achieved. 
 
The tests performed on20170 investigated 25% C2H4/75% He issuing into 30% O2/He and 
21% O 2/He. At 5 and 5.5 cc/s, nice blue chemiluminescent flames were ignited, but 
eventually were cut off because of the burner temperature limit being reached. At 6 cc/s, 
a nice blue flame was ignited which expanded slowly to extinction. At 7, 10, and 15 cc/s, 
sooty ignition occurred, but as the flames expanded, the soot went away, eventually 
resulting in radiative extinction. By ra mping the flow rates up, starting at 5 cc/s, soot at 
ignition was minimized, and the flames could expand to extinction. Ramp down of the 
flow rate resulted in almost immediate extinction. For tests at 21% O 2/He atmosphere, 
cases at 5, 10, and 15 cc/s res ulted in flames that expanded quickly to extinction. Less 
soot was present at ignition compared with that for the 30% O 2/He atmosphere cases. 
Consistent ignition was not always achieved for the same conditions, which is puzzling. 
 
Testing on 20176 explored 30% C2H4/70% He issuing into 30% O2/He and 21% O2/He. At 
5 cc/s, a long duration flame was established that eventually reached the burner 
temperature limit. At 6, 7, 10, and 15 cc/s, the flames were sooty at ignition, but the soot 
dissipated; and they expanded to extinction. Ramping up the flow rates, starting at 5 cc/s, 
minimized soot at ignition and resulted in flames that slowly expanded to extinction. For 
tests at 21% O 2/He atmosphere, cases at 5, 10, and 15 cc/s resulted in flames that 
expanded to extinction. At 4 cc/s, the flame lasted a while before eventual extinction. 
The 3 cc/s case did not ignite. Ramp down of the flow rate seemed to result in flames 
that extinguished quickly before the protocol could ramp down the flow rate. 
 
The last testing of Round 2, which was a makeup of 20155, occurred on 20190, with 45% 
H2/55% He issuing into 30% O 2/He and 21% O 2/He. For both oxygen concentration 
environments, flow rates resulting in expanding flames lasted for a while, but were cut 
off by automated protocol before self-extinction when the burner temperature limit was 
reached. As for cases where the flow rates were ramped down, extinction detection was 
observed for both oxygen concentration environments. We are currently analyzing the 
data to determine if extinction was kinetic or due to heat loss to the burner. A last set of 
tests were conducted with a reduced oxygen concentration atmosphere, i.e., 17.5% 
O2/82.5% He. Some cases indicated that radiative and kinetic extinction were possibly 
observed. 
 
In summary, selected preliminary findings from this testing include: 
o Cases run for nitrogen-diluted methane and ethylene flames and in air seemed to 
indicate kinetic extinction at low flow rates and radiative extinction at high flow 
rates. As previ ously m entioned above (and in our report for the preceding 
increment pair), such phenomena were not observed in our ground -based 
research, given the limited microgravity durations. Nevertheless, comparisons 
with computational simulations are needed to ass ess bet ter the extinction 
behavior.

title: s_Flame_final_report_20210729
text:
ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 29 July 2021 
70 
 
o Cases run for nitrogen-diluted hydrogen flames seemed to show kinetic extinction 
at ramp down. However, for the mass flow rates that could be accommodated, 
radiative extinction was not observed. 
o Cases run for nitrogen -diluted hydrogen/methane mixture flames manifested 
extinction, which are presumed to be radiative. However, kinetic extinction at low 
flow rates could not be identified. More analyses of the data are needed. 
o Cases for helium -diluted cases shifted the ex tinction limits with respect to the 
nitrogen-diluted cases. In general, kinetic extinction was difficult to observe for 
the conditions examined. More analyses are needed to assess instability near the 
flame limits, which was predicted to occur computationally.

text:
ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 29 July 2021 
75 
 
Appendix G. ISS Operations per the Payload Weekly Science Summary 
This section is from Dennis Stocker’s log of ACME operations. 
 
s-Flame round 1, featuring nitrogen dilution 
 
2019 
Week 21: July 26 – August 1 
On GMT 206, we performed the final test points for the first round of testing for ACME Flame Design. Test 
points were performed using ethylene fuel (sometimes diluted) in a chamber environment of air (21% 
oxygen, 79% nitrogen at 1 atm). The flames for these tests were short -lived and non-sooty—unlike the 
flames from the tests at higher oxygen concentrations. The goal of Flame Design is to improve our 
understanding of soot processes so that flames can be “designed” to be soot free. 
 
To prepare for the start of ACME s-Flame (Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames), Christina 
Koch replaced the bottles on CIR Manifolds #2 and #4 on GMT 211. While monitoring the bottle pressures, 
it was noted that the pressure of the bottle at Manifold #4 was slowly decreasing. The rack was powered 
down, and Nick Hague an d Luca Parmitano both helped with troubleshooting operations. Currently, a 
forward plan is being developed. 
 
Week 22: August 2 - 8 
On GMT 219, Luca Parmitano replaced the CIR Manifold #4 bottle, which was losing pressure while 
installed and the valve opene d, with a known good bottle. While monitoring, the known good bottle 
maintained its pressure! Next week, we plan to continue transitioning to the next ACME experiment, s-
Flame (Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames). 
 
Week 23: August 9 - 15 
On GMT 225, Christina Koch configured the ACME Chamber Insert and the CIR Combustion Chamber to 
support the next ACME experiment, s-Flame (Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames). 
 
 
Week 27: September 6 - 12 
On GMT 254, the first test points were performed for ACME s-Flame (Structure and Response of Spherical 
Diffusion Flames) with 13 spherical flames ignited. This investigation is the fifth to be conducted as part 
of the ACME project, which features studies of burner-stabilized flames of gaseous fuels. s-Flame’s goal is 
to advance our ability to predict the structure and dynamics, including extinction, of both soot -free and 
sooty flames—where today’s testing was focused on soot-free flames. Without the buoyant flows created 
by Earth’s gravity, flames in microgravity are typically spherical, which allows the analysis to focus on the 
combustion chemistry and details of the transport phenomena. 
 
CAPTION TO VIDEO, WHICH IS NOT INCLUDED IN THIS LOG 
In this test point video, a non-sooty (blue) flame is ignited with a retracting hot-wire igniter, where 
the gaseous fuel is flowing from a porous spherical burner. After ignition, the flame grows slightly 
as a result of the diminishing oxygen gradient. An array of 14-micron ceramic fibers is then moved 
toward the flame, where the temperature of the flame can be determined from the color of the 
fiber’s glow—where yellow is hotter than orange, and orange is hotter than red. While only a 
single fiber can be seen at first, a s econd becomes visible when the fla me suddenly gets bigger

title: s_Flame_final_report_20210729
text:
ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 29 July 2021 
76 
 
and engulfs the first fiber. The diluted ethylene flow to the burner was abruptly increased and 
made to be more fuel rich. As a result, the flame needed to grow to reach enough oxygen to burn 
all the fuel. 
 
Throughout the test, the spherical flame is open near the burner’s tube because of heat loss. As 
the flame grows, the opening around the tube increases (while the flame weakens and dims). The 
flame edge then pulls away from the burner tube and leaves just a small portion of the spherical 
shell. This large hole in the flame shell allows for fuel and air mixing and the flame momentarily 
reestablishes and brightens before it extinguishes. 
 
Week 28: September 13 - 19 
On GMT 256, 16 spherical flames were successfully ignited for ACME s-Flame (Structure and Response of 
Spherical Diffusion Flames). Even though ethylene’s double bond tends to make it a sooty fuel, these 
nitrogen-diluted ethylene flames were all non-sooty (except for during ignition). For each test point, the 
harp-like array of 14 -micron ceramic fibers was used to determine temperatures in or near the flame, 
while an array of thermocouples was used to measure the spread of the thermal field from the flame. 
 
ACME Flame Design Images 
 
These two images are of the same flame at nearly the same time. The image on the left is a false-colored 
image. The porous spherical burner can be seen in the middle of the flame. The flame shell surrounds the 
burner except at the fuel supply tube, which causes t he flame to locally quench because of heat loss. A 
glowing ceramic fiber can be seen above the flame, where the fiber’s glow is used to determine the local 
temperature by comparison of the red, green, and blue color planes in a measurement technique known 
as pyrometry. The faint lines at the top of the flame suggest that the fiber may have locally quenched the 
flame even though it was above the flame. 
 
The image on the right is from an intensified camera looking at the emission from the excited molecule 
CH*, which emits a photon of blue 431-nm light when it drops to a lower energy state in a process referred 
to as chemiluminescence. The location of the burner sphere is noticeable due to the diminished light in 
the middle of the flame. The opening in the flam e shell due to the burner’s tube i s also noticeable. The

title: s_Flame_final_report_20210729
text:
ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 29 July 2021 
77 
 
apparent opening in the top of the flame may be caused by the fiber array arm, which, in this camera’s 
view, blocks the flame. 
In microgravity, flames aren’t supplied oxygen through buoyant convention. As a result, low-momentum 
flames like these in a quiescent (still) atmosphere tend to be quite weak and self-extinguish. Microgravity 
is an extremely useful for environment for this experiment since a key objective is to study flame dynamics 
and extinction. 
 
Week 29: September 20 - 26 
On GMT 266, Luca Parmitano replaced the ACME Fuel Controller and the bottles at CIR Manifold #2 and 
CIR Manifold #4. These changes support the next ACME s -Flame test points, which will be in a chamber 
environment of air (21% oxygen, 79% nitrogen at 1 atm) and will use diluted methane fuel at faster flow 
rates. 
 
Week 5: October 25 - 31 
On GMT 297 on the back of the CIR Optics Bench, Jessica Meir removed a failed hard drive from the FCF 
Image Processor and then replaced the FCF Image Processor. On GMT 301, the CIR was powered up and 
a checkout of the new FCF Image Processor was successful. We returned to performing test points later 
in the week! 
 
Week 6: November 1 - 7 
On GMT 304 and 308, 30 spherical flames were successfully ignited for ACME s -Flame (Structure and 
Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames). These tests burned methane fuel diluted with nitrogen in 
atmospheres of 21% and 30% oxygen (with a balance of nitrogen). Methane is the primary component of 
natural gas. These test points focused on determining where the radiative heat loss or velocities are too 
high for the flame to be sustained, which are known as the radiative and convective extinction limits. 
Radiative heat transport is much more important unde r microgravity conditions because the hot gases 
don’t buoyantly rise from the flame. 
 
ACME s-Flame Images 
 
This figure shows three flames of 45% methane burning in 30% oxygen. The gaseous methane fuel flows 
from the porous sphere of the burner, which is v isible in the flame’s center. The flow of fuel increases 
from left to right, which increases the size of the flame. The burner’s fuel supply tube is visible below the 
sphere. The flame loses heat to this tube causing an opening, which typically grows with time as the flame 
weakens. In the flame on the right, the opening is comparatively small, which signifies a stronger flame.

In the left and center images, the glow of a 14-micron ceramic fiber is visible above the flame. Where the 
fiber is visibly glowing, the flame’s temperature at that point can be determined via color-ratio pyrometry, 
which uses a color camera characterized for that purpose. The faint glow of a second fiber further from 
the flame can be seen at the top of the center image. When the image on the right was captured, the fiber 
array was not yet inserted into the flame. 
 
Week 8: November 15 - 21 
On GMT 323, Drew Morgan replaced the bottles at CIR Manifold #2 and CIR Manifold #4 to support ACME 
s-Flame test points using pure hydrogen fuel in air (21% oxygen, 79% nitrogen at 1 atm). 
 
Week 12: December 13 - 19 
On GMT 347, Drew Morgan replaced the ACME Bypass and Fuel Controllers to support the ACME s-Flame 
(Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames) test points on GMT 352, which flowe d nitrogen 
and fuel at slower flow rates. 
 
Ten flames were successfully ignited on GMT 352. These tests were conducted with nitrogen -diluted 
hydrogen fuel making the flames very faint. The CIR is equipped with an intensified camera, which images 
these very faint flames by visualizing the ultraviolet emission of the OH molecule (at 310 nm) as it drops 
to a lower energy level. This process is known as chemiluminescence. Thus far, there has only been a 
preliminary review of some image data. These tests used h ydrogen fuel in differing concentrations with 
both steady and ramped flow rates. The tests with ramped flow rates investigated extinction 
characteristics of the flame. 
 
Week 14: December 27 - January 2 
On GMT 358, Luca Parmitano replaced the ACME Bypass and Fuel Controllers to support ACME s -Flame 
(Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames) test points with faster nitrogen and fuel flow rates. 
 
On GMT 002, Oleg Skripochka and Luca Parmitano replaced the bottle at CIR Manifold #4 to support ACME 
s-Flame test points using a hydrogen/methane fuel mixture in air (21% oxygen, 79% nitrogen at 1 atm). 
 
2020 
Week 15: January 3 - 9 
On GMT 006, 17 flames were successfully ignited for ACME s-Flame (Structure and Response of Spherical 
Diffusion Flames), which uses spherically -symmetric diffusion flames t o investigate fundamental 
processes, such as flame extinction. These tests were cond ucted with a mixture of hydrogen (20%), 
methane (25%), and nitrogen (55%) ejected from the porous spherical burner into a chamber atmosphere 
of air (21% oxygen, 79% nitroge n at 1 atm). The dim, soot -free flames exhibited local quenching due to 
radiative heat loss and reignition, which sometimes occurred repeatedly. In these cases, the dynamic parts 
of the broken flame sometimes appear to dance around the burner. 
 
CAPTION TO VIDEO, WHICH IS NOT INCLUDED IN THIS LOG 
In this test point video, a non-sooty (blue) flame is ignited with a retracting hot-wire igniter. The 
harp-like array of 14 -micron ceramic fibers moves in from the left to a fixed position. The glow 
from the fibers allows for a good estimation of the local temperature. The flame starts “dancing,” 
where it partially quenches due to radiative heat loss and the remaining flame stretches and 
circles around the burner through a repeated combination of quenching and reign ition. The fuel

title: s_Flame_final_report_20210729
text:
ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 29 July 2021 
79 
 
and oxygen, which are normally separated by the flame, mix where the flame quenches, making 
the local gas more flammable. 
 
Week 16: January 10 - 16 
On GMT 013, 22 flames were successfully ignited for ACME s-Flame (Structure and Response of Spherical 
Diffusion Flames), which is a record number of sustained flames in a single day of testing for all the ACME 
experiments! Like the tests performed on GMT 006, these tests burned a mixture of hydrogen, methane, 
and nitrogen but with a greater hyd rogen concentration relative to the methane concentration. Even 
though these flames were less dynamic than the “dancing” flames from GMT 006, they did break apart 
and create flamelets. The flamelets were about 1 cm across and were shaped like curved bands or circles 
rather than spheres or ellipsoids. 
 
 
This figure shows four different tests from GMT 013, where the flow rate of the hydrogen/methane fuel 
increases from left to right while the nitrogen flow rate remains constant. The burner, with its supply tube 
and porous sphere, is opposite the flame. The fuel and nitrogen both flow from the burner sphere into a 
chamber atmosphere of ~19% oxygen and nitrogen at a pressure of ~1 atm. 
 
The bright horizontal lines in each flame are the glowing 14 -micron ceramic fibers, where that glow can 
be used to determine the flame’s temperature. As the fuel flow rate increases, the flames become larger 
and separate flamelets form. For these tests, the flow rate was increased to explore flame stability and 
extinction limits. 
 
Week 17: January 17 - 23 
On GMT 017, Oleg Skripochka replaced the bottles at CIR M anifold #2 and CIR Manifold #4 to support 
ACME s-Flame test points using pure hydrogen fuel in air (21% oxygen, 79% nitrogen at 1 atm). 
 
Week 18: January 24 - 30 
On GMT 024, 16 flames were successfully ignited for ACME s-Flame (Structure and Response of Spherical 
Diffusion Flames). These tests were conducted with nitrogen -diluted hydrogen fuel making the flames 
very faint. Even though the flames were barely visible, their pr esence was obvious due to the 
measurements of various instrumentation, including thermocouples, radiometers, and photomultiplier 
tubes. The glowing ceramic fibers were also a positive indication of a flame. The harp -like array of 14 -
micron ceramic fibers w as translated into the flame to make optical measurements of the flame 
temperature from the hot fibers’ visible glow. 
 
Week 19: January 31 - February 6 
On GMT 029, 21 flames were successfully ignited for ACME s-Flame (Structure and Response of Spherical 
Diffusion Flames). These were the final tests for the first round of testing for s-Flame. In this round, a total

text:
ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 29 July 2021 
80 
 
of 145 flames were ignited using nitrogen-diluted gaseous fuels. In the upcoming second round, tests will 
be conducted with the same fuels but diluted with helium, which has much different transport properties 
than nitrogen. 
 
CAPTION TO VIDEO, WHICH IS NOT INCLUDED IN THIS LOG 
In this test point video, a sooty (yellow) flame is ignited with a retracting hot -wire igniter. This 
flame is burning ethylene fuel diluted by nitrogen. Ethylene’s double bond tends to make flames 
sooty. However, the soot (which is black, but thermally glows yellow) quickly disappears, leaving 
a blue soot-free spherical flame. 
 
Following ignition, the flame grows to reach eno ugh oxygen to consume the fuel. The harp -like 
array of 14 -micron ceramic fibers moves in from the left to a fixed position. The glow from the 
fibers allows for a good estimation of the local temperature. These flames are a bit like bubbles, 
where the fuel is within the flame, the oxygen is outside of it, and the light , heat, and chemical 
products are emitted at the surface where they come together and react. 
 
The base of the flame begins to retreat from the burner’s fuel supply tube due to heat loss. Both 
the flame and the glowing fibers can be seen to dim as the flame weakens. Eventually the base of 
the flame begins to oscillate. The flame locally quenches—creating a hole in the flame. This hole 
allows for increased mixing of the fuel and oxygen, which in turn allows the flame to temporarily 
recover. As the oscillations grow in strength, the flame goes out. 
 
s-Flame round 2, featuring helium dilution 
 
Week 2: April 17 - 23 
On GMT 114, Chris Cassidy replaced the CIR FOMA Cal Unit on the back of the CIR Optics Bench. This 
activity allowed us to perform the calibration of the CIR’s FOMA (Fuel/Oxidizer Management As sembly) 
system. This calibration needs to be completed yearly to ensure that all the pressure transducers in the 
CIR are accurate. 
 
On GMT 115, in support of the CIR FOMA Calibration, Chris Cas sidy closed and opened valves on the gas 
bottles installed in CIR. 
 
Week 3: April 24 - 30 
On GMT 119, Chris Cassidy replaced the ACME Fuel Controller and set the CIR Valve Timers to support the 
upcoming second round of testing for ACME s -Flame (Structure a nd Response of Spherical Diffusion 
Flames) starting in a couple weeks. 
 
s-Flame’s goal is to advance our ability to predict the structure and dynamics, including extinction, of both 
soot-free and sooty flames. Without the buoyant flows created by Earth’s gravity, flames in microgravity 
are typically spherical, which allows the analysis to focus on the combustion chemistry and details of the 
transport phenomena. Results may lead to more efficient and less polluting combustion technology for 
use on Earth.

text:

ACME s-Flame Test Point Image 
 
In this false-colored preliminary image, the flame encompasses the porous spherical burner and its fuel 
supply tube. The bright lines at the to p are 14 -micron ceramic fibers that are glowing because of the 
flame’s heat. Where the fibers are visibly glowing, the flame’s temperature at that point can be 
determined by color -ratio pyrometry, which uses a color camera characterized for that purpose. 
Qualitatively, a yellow glow is hotter than orange, which is in turn hotter than red —just like metal in a 
forge. Given the extremely fine fibers, the measurement effectively provides the flame temperature, 
which can be compared with the results of computational modeling. 
 
s-Flame’s goal is to advance our ability to predict the structure and dynamics, including extinction, of both 
soot-free and sooty flames. Without the buoyant flows created by Earth’s gravity, flames in microgravity 
are typically spherical, which allows the analysis to focus on the combustion chemistry and details of the 
transport phenomena. Results may lead to more efficient and less polluting combustion technology for 
use on Earth.

On GMT 142, 17 flames were successfully ignited for ACME s-Flame (Structure and Response of Spherical 
Diffusion Flames). These tests burned a hydrogen/methane fuel mixture diluted with helium but with a 
different ratio of flammable gases than investigated in the first two test days. These tests were performed 
in a chamber environment of 30% oxygen (the remainder was helium); whereas, the first two test days 
were performed in 21% oxygen. Flames are strongly dependent on the oxygen concentration, so these 
flames lasted longer before extinguishing than the earlier tests. On GMT 147, Anatoly Ivanishin replaced

in from the left to a fixed position. The glow from the fibers allows for a good estimation of the 
local temperature. As the flame opens, the fuel and oxygen, which are normally separated by the

Week 8: May 29 - June 4 
In support of ACME s -Flame (Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames) test points, Chris 
Cassidy replaced the ACME Igniter Tip and the ACME Fuel Controller on GMT 154. The next day, nine 
helium-diluted hydrogen flames were successfully ignited for s -Flame, where most of these tests were 
performed in a chamber environment of ~30% oxygen with a balance of helium. Previously, similar tests 
were performed with nitrogen dilution, but helium is dramatically different than nitrogen. Helium is more 
diffusive and has a greater thermal conductivity than nitrogen. Studying these differences can enable new 
learning, particularly when combined with the microgravity environment. On GMT 156, Anatoly Ivanishin 
replaced the bottle at CIR Manifold #4 to support ACME s -Flame test points using methane fuel diluted 
with helium. 
 
ACME s-Flame Test Point Image 
 
One benefit of performing combustion research in microgravity is spherical flames. T his image 
(preliminary and false -colored) shows a spherical flame of diluted hydrogen ~25 mm in diameter. 
Reducing the flame geometry to a single dimension dramatically simplifies analysis and modeling. It also 
enables computation focused on chemical kinetics and transport phenomena rather than fluid dynamics 
and flame structure.

title: s_Flame_final_report_20210729
text:
ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 29 July 2021 
84 
 
The two bright lines above the flame are 14 -micron ceramic fibers, which are visibly glowing because of 
the flame’s heat. The temperature distribution along the glowing fiber can be quantified through Thin 
Filament Pyrometry, where the hue is indicative of the temperature. Flame measurements are also made 
with intensified cameras, thermopile detectors, photomultiplier tubes, and thermocouples. All this data 
is used to improve and v alidate flame modeling and through that enable improvements in practical 
terrestrial combustion. 
 
Week 9: June 5 - 11 
On GMT 160, 12 helium-diluted methane flames were ignited in oxygen/helium atmospheres for ACME s-
Flame (Structure and Response of Spheric al Diffusion Flames). Compared to other gaseous hydrocarbon 
fuels, methane (CH4) is more difficult to ignite because of its lack of carbon -carbon bonds. Methane 
ignition hadn’t been an issue in earlier testing with nitrogen dilution, but it was challenging in this week’s 
tests because of helium’s much greater thermal conductivity. Nonetheless, the recently installed coiled 
igniter tip enabled us to ignite these flames. 
 
The results from the current series of s -Flame tests will be compared with the results from the previous 
tests using nitrogen dilution. In that earlier testing, it was found that radiative extinction (i.e., extinction 
caused by radiative heat loss) is a common event, which had been predicted computationally. However, 
we did not observe this in preliminary ground-based testing. It was also seen in the on -orbit tests that 
radiative reabsorption extends the flame size at extinction. Another type of extinction was sometimes 
observed, where the gas velocities caused nitrogen-diluted ethylene flames (under certain conditions) to 
blow out. It will be interesting to see what the future comparisons will reveal about the nature of flames. 
 
On GMT 162, Anatoly Ivanishin replaced the bottle at CIR Manifold #4 to support ACME s-Flame test points 
using 20% ethylene fuel diluted with helium. 
 
Week 10: June 12 - 18 
On GMT 164, 11 helium-diluted ethylene flames were ignited for ACME s-Flame (Structure and Response 
of Spherical Diffusion Flames). This is a shift in testing for the s -Flame experiment from non-sooty fuels 
(i.e., hydrogen, methane, or hydrogen/methane blends) to a sooty fuel. Ethylene (C2H4) tends to be a 
sooty fuel because it has a carbon double -bond. Soot forms when hot fuel combines with itself in the 
absence of oxygen, where the union of fuel mo lecules is facilitated by the double bond. The flames in 
these tests were sooty at ignition, but the soot quickly disappeared resulting in blue flames, where blue 
is the natural color of flames with hydrocarbon fuels. On GMT 168, Anatoly Ivanishin replaced the bottles 
at CIR Manifold #1, CIR Manifold #2 and CIR Manifold #4 to support ACME s-Flame test points using 25% 
ethylene fuel diluted with helium. 
 
CAPTION TO VIDEO, WHICH IS NOT INCLUDED IN THIS LOG 
This test point video runs at half speed to better show what is happening with the flame. A flame 
of 20% ethylene fuel ignites in a chamber atmosphere of about 30% oxygen (both diluted with 
helium). The flame is initially very bright. Although the soot particles are black, their glow depends 
on their temperature, where yellow is hotter than orange which is in turn hotter than red. While 
some soot clusters escape the flame, much of the soot becomes trapped within the flame by the 
temperature gradient. 
 
After some time, the array of ceramic fibers is transla ted into the flame to determine the radial 
temperature distribution where the fibers are glowing. Despite their 14 -micron diameter, the

title: s_Flame_final_report_20210729
text:
ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 29 July 2021 
85 
 
fibers appear to cool or push away the soot because that side of the flame becomes increasingly 
blue. 
 
The flame becomes all blue and retreats from the fuel supply tube because of heat loss. The 
opening in the flame allows fuel and oxygen to directly mix, where they are normally separated 
by the presence of the flame shell. This mixing enhances flammability and the reinvigorated and 
locally brighter flame flashes back to the supply tube reestablishing the nominally spherical flame. 
But it is short-lived, and the flame quickly retreats again until it is just a “cap” on the left. Mixing 
again leads to another flame flash, but it quickly extinguishes due to radiative heat loss, heat loss 
to the supply tube, and conductive heat loss enhanced by the helium’s high thermal conductivity. 
 
Week 11: June 19 - 25 
 
On GMT 170, 20 fl ames were ignited for ACME s -Flame (Structure and Respo nse of Spherical Diffusion 
Flames). These flames burned a 25% ethylene/75% helium blend; whereas, the flames on GMT 164 burned 
a 20% ethylene/80% helium blend. Comparing these data will enable analysis of the effects of this 
fuel/inert blend on flame dynam ics, such as extinction behavior and structure. On GMT 171, Anatoly 
Ivanishin replaced the bottle at CIR Manifold #4 to support ACME s -Flame test points using a 30% 
ethylene/70% helium blend. 
 
ACME s-Flame Test Point Image 
 
In this image (preliminary and false-colored), the flame on the right has a higher ethylene concentration 
than the flame on the left. As expected, the flame on the right is larger where the spherical flame expands 
until the fuel reaches enough oxygen to be consumed. 
 
These flames, which are non-premixed, are like bubbles in that the gaseous fuel is inside the bubble and 
the oxygen is outside the bubble. The flame shell, like the film of a bubble, is a thin sheet where the fuel 
and oxygen come together and react, producing light, heat, and chemical products, such as carbon dioxide 
and water vapor. Meanwhile, the helium —which readily diffuses —is free to cross the flame shell.

title: s_Flame_final_report_20210729
text:
ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 29 July 2021 
86 
 
However, diffusion was minimal because the helium concentrations within the fuel and the surrounding 
atmosphere were similar. 
 
Both flames were bright and sooty at ignition, but these images are from late in each test when the flames 
became dim. The bright lines at the top are the 14 -micron ceramic fibers used for optical determination 
of the flame temperature using a camera characterized for that purpose. 
 
s-Flame’s goal is to advance our ability to predict the structure and dynamics, including extinction, of both 
soot-free and sooty flames. Without the buoyant flows created by Earth’s gravity, flames in microgravity 
are typically spherical, which allows the analysis to focus on the combustion chemistry and details of the 
transport phenomena. Results may le ad to more efficient and less polluting combustion technology for 
use on Earth. 
 
Week 12: June 26 - July 2 
GMT 176 was a record-breaking day for ACME with 23 flames ignited—the most we’ve ignited in one day! 
We’ve now ignited over 250 flames for s -Flame (Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames) 
and over 1000 flames for ACME since it started in Nov. 2017. The tests on GMT 176 were performed with 
30% ethylene in helium for comparison with the results from the two preceding test days, which burned 
20% and 25% ethylene/helium blends. 
 
CAPTION TO VIDEO, WHICH IS NOT INCLUDED IN THIS LOG 
In this test poi nt video, helium-diluted ethylene fuel is ignited with a low fuel flow rate to limit 
the soot produced with ignition. After ignition, the flow rate is tripled in a smooth ramp, so that 
the flame response can be observed. As expected, the flame quickly grows, where it must expand 
to reach enough oxygen to consume all the fuel. 
 
Before the fuel flow rate has completely tripled, the flame retreats from the burner’s fuel supply 
tube because of heat loss —creating a hole in the flame near the tube. This hole al lows fo r 
increased mixing of the ethylene and oxygen, which are normally separated by the flame shell. 
This mixing causes the flame to momentarily reestablish around the burner tube with a bright 
flash of light. Mixing again leads to another flame flash, a fter which the flame fully extinguishes. 
The fuel flow rate did completely triple before the flame extinguished. 
 
Although not visible in the video, the measured OH* and CH* chemiluminescence was relatively 
constant throughout this test with the important exceptions of ignition and the bright flashes of 
light prior to extinction. In contrast, the measured chemiluminescence declined with time in 
similar tests with constant fuel flow rates. OH* and CH* are molecules at an elevated energy state 
which emit a photon of a specific wavelength as their energy level drops a level. The CH* emission 
is the source of most of the blue in a hydrocarbon flame, while the OH* emission is in the 
ultraviolet. ACME uses the latter measurement as an indicator of ignition and extinction because 
it is insensitive to the hot-wire igniter and hot burned gases. 
 
Using this unique microgravity data, the s -Flame investigation seeks to test and improve 
computational models, which may enable improvements to practical combustion on Earth.

In the afternoon, Cassidy moved over to the U.S. Destiny laboratory module and swapped computer parts

design advanced fuel transfer systems and increase fire safety.

Rack to enable safe fuel and flame science.

Preps 
Today, the three NASA astronauts and two Roscosmos cosmonauts juggled a variety of experiments 
encompassing fluids, combustion, genetics and vision among others. … Russian Flight Engineer Anatoly 
Ivanishin … swapped fuel bottles inside the Combustion Integrated Rack to continue safe fuel and flame 
research. 
 
2020 June 16 - Biology and Physics as Crew Enters BEAM, Preps for Spacewalk 
Tuesday’s science aboard the International Space Station encompassed life science, fluids and flames to 
help humans on Earth and in space. … Veteran cosmonaut Anatoly Ivanishin continued to service 
the Combustion Integrated Rack replacing fuel bottles to maintain safe fuel and flame research in the 
device. Insights could improve fire safety as well as combustion processes for Earth and space industries. 
 
2020 June 19 - Crew Readies Satellite and Organizes Station 
Cosmonaut Anatoly Ivanishin changed out fuel bottles in the Combustion Integrated Rack this morning to 
continue the safe research of flames in microgravity. 
 
2020 June 22 – Astronauts Check Spacewalk Tools and Suits, Study Space Physics 
Hurley spent the first half of his Monday working on fluid and combustion physics. He first explored 
how microfluidics can cause biochemical reactions in blood revealing mechanisms hidden on Earth. Next, 
he researched fabricating composite materials to learn how to repair and build structures on future space 
missions. 
While Hurley worked on fluid physics, the reference to combustion is presumably in error. At the least, he 
did not work on the ACME project on that day, if at all. 
 
2020 July 6 - Cargo and Science Operations Start Work Week 
Cosmonaut Anatoly Ivanishin replaced fuel bottles inside the Combustion Integrated Rack to continue 
safe fuel and flame research.

text:
ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 29 July 2021 
106 
 
Appendix M. Summary of the ISS data collection 
The s-Flame data is all digital and includes both image and non-image data, where this is true for the other 
ACME experiments. To be clear, there was no collection of soot or other physical samples that were 
subsequently transported to the ground. 
 
The s-Flame image data includes images from the following cameras: 
1. ACME DataCam, used with a clear fused -silica ‘filter’ and various zoom and focus settings (but 
those settings were consistent within each individual test) 
2. CFI intensified camera, used with CH*, formaldehyde, and UV fused silica filters, but where only 
a single filter was used in each test 
3. Low Light Level Ultraviolet (LLL-UV) camera, equipped with an OH* filter 
4. High-Bitdepth Multispectral (HiBMs) camera , equipped with a red filter corresponding to the 
opposing CIR illumination package, which was sometimes left off 
The raw DataCam images are in a Halcon Iconic Object (hobj) format, while the images from the CFI , 
HiBMs, and LLL-UV cameras are provided in a Tagged Image File (tif) format. In contrast, the analog video 
was recorded on the ground in a Transport Stream (ts) format. 
 
The key non-imaging data from a test is a comma-delimited file that is described in detail in the Software 
Interface Design Description (ACME-DOC-010 Rev. D). 
 
The raw data is currently archived at NASA and work is underway to make it available publicly through 
NASA’s Physical Science Informatics System (PSI).

Both Princeton and Rutgers have promoted awareness of the s-Flame investigation online, for

Experiments from a Rutgers Office.” 
 
Meanwhile, NASA promoted awareness of ISS combustion research with the video ‘The Power of 
Studying Combustion on the ISS’ which was posted on March 13, 2018. 
 
Awareness of ISS combustion research, including the ACME project, was promoted on Oct. 15, 2018 
by The Combustion Institute in their online news article, “International Space Station (ISS) Combustion 
Experiments.” 
 
Stocker is involved in a broad range of NASA educational outreach to students and teachers, Scouts 
of both genders, and the general publi c. His primary outreach focus is the fundamentals of 
microgravity (for which resources are available via http://tinyurl.com/SEECmicrogravity) and human 
spaceflight. But he periodically addresses other topics, e.g., where he sometimes speaks on ‘NASA 
and the Science of Superman’ – for example at the Superman Celebration in Metropolis, IL. In this 
regard, his NASA outreach is carried out locally, regionally, nationally, and online. For example, he 
regularly presents on microgravity at Space Center Houston’s Space Exploration Edu cators 
Conference (SEEC). He has exhibited the last five National Scout Jamborees, four national Boy Scout 
conferences, the last three national Girl Scout conventions, and the 2019 World Scout Jamboree 
(which was held in the U.S.). Stocker has been a key lead for the agency in NASA’s participation in 
these Scouting events, where as an example the latter outreach is visually described at

text:
2 
 
 
The data is generally explained through 2 excerpts from the Software IDD, i.e., 
Software Interface Design Description, ACME-DOC-010 Rev C (August 2016) 
 8. Output Files 
 4. Internal Interfaces (which includes Tables 15-17*) 
*where Table 17 describes channels A0-4 of the DNx-AO-333 analog output board as discussed in 8.1 below. 
 
8.0 Output FILES 
8.1 Data Output File 
Data output files are created using the SystemOpenTestPoint command which creates a file named and stored at 
/payload/sci/testpointName_x/testpointName_x_data.csv, where testpointName is the parameter received in the 
SystemOpenTestPoint command and _x is optional to avoid duplicate files, where x = 1,2,3, etc. 
The file contains a two-line header. The first line has the date and time, documentation of the setup received in a 
SystemDefineSetup command, and the PMT gains. The second line has the column headings for the subsequent rows of data. The 
text of the column headings is defined by the Diagnostics/Header registry entry or the Diagnostics/BreHeader entry depending on 
whether the SystemDefineSetup command experimentType parameter was BRE or not. The column headings should match the data 
which is the following: 
- A timestamp in the format HH:MM:SS:mmm, where mmm is milliseconds. 
- 11 channels of analog input from the cube DNx-AI-207 board in the order shown in Table 1. 
- 25 channels of analog input from the cube DNx-AI-225 board in the order shown in Table 2. (The names of 
many of these values change depending on whether it is a BRE test or not, hence the two options for header.) 
- Channel AO-4 of the DNx-AO-333 analog output board. This is the E-Field control voltage. 
Rows of comma-separated data is added to the file between DataRecordingStart and DataRecordingStop commands at a 
rate defined by the Diagnostics/SampleTimeMsec registry entry, see Error! Reference source not found., defaulting to 8 
msec for 125 Hz sampling.

title: ACME non-imaging data file description
cite: PSI-23_Science Documents_ACME non-imaging data file description.pdf, p. 3
text:
3 
 
8.2 Message Log File 
Software messages are logged to files named and stored at /payload/logs/YYYY-MM-DD_hh-mmACME.log, where YYYY 
is year, MM is month, DD is day of month, hh is hour, and mm is minutes. The date in the name is when the log file is 
created, soon after software startup. 
Each message line in the file begins with a timestamp and a logging category. The timestamp is of the format YYYY-MM-
DD DDD hh:mm:ss:mmm, where DDD is day of the year, mmm is milliseconds, and the rest are self-explanatory. See 
section Error! Reference source not found. for information about the logging category and how to filter them out if 
desired. 
8.3 Command Log File 
The message log file, section 8.2, includes messages showing commands received and their parameters. Command log 
files contain only the details of each command received. The files are named and stored at /payload/logs/YYYY-MM-
DD_hh-mmACMECommands.log. The format is for each command received a timestamped line of text with the 
command name followed by timestamped lines of text showing each parameter name and parameter value, including 
header information.

title: ACME s-Flame  DoD
text:
PSI Data Organization Document 
Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) Structure and Response of Spherical 
Diffusion Flames (s-Flame) 
 
1 
 
To gain an initial understanding of this experiment, refer to the documents “ACME non-imaging data file 
description.pdf” and “s-Flame_final_report_20210729.pdf” located in “Final Report” of the “Resulting Products” 
section on the “Pubs & Docs” tab. 
 
The s-Flame data is organized in PSI by diluent and fuel composition. Raw data, and video & image data are 
available on the “Scientific Data and Information Tab” of each of the eight “Experiment Data” records: 
 
 1 Nitrogen-diluted Hydrogen and Oxygen 
 2 Nitrogen-diluted Methane and Oxygen 
 3 Nitrogen-diluted Hydrogen-Methane mixtures and Oxygen 
 4 Nitrogen-diluted Ethylene and Oxygen 
 5 Helium-diluted Hydrogen and Oxygen 
 6 Helium-diluted Methane and Oxygen 
 7 Helium-diluted Hydrogen-Methane mixtures and Oxygen 
 8 Helium-diluted Ethylene and Oxygen 
 
Within each “Experiment Data” record, “Raw Data”, “Images” and “Audio/Video Files” are available on the 
“Scientific Data and Information” tab. Test names are formatted YYDDDX# where YY identifies year, DDD identifies 
day of year (GMT), X identifies a letter and # identifies a number – where the different numbers can be for repeats 
but are typically variants, e.g., with different flow rate(s) or instrumentation setting(s), e.g. 19308F1. Record 
naming and listings are based on the detailed information in the test conditions table below (page 2). 
 
Test specific raw data files are located on the “Raw Data and Information” tab of the “Raw & Analyzed Data” 
record. The first row of the .csv files provides information about the test configuration. The headers of the basic 
data in .csv files is explained in Section 10.1, beginning on page 126 of the “ACME-DOC-010 Rev D.pdf” located in 
the “Data Organization Document(s)” section of the “Scientific Data and Information” section on the “Data” tab of 
the ACME s-Flames “Investigations” record. Associated videos are located on the “General” tab and associated 
images are located on the “Image Data and Information” tab of the “Videos & Images” record. 
 
There are various other supporting engineering documents, videos, reports and publications available on the other 
tabs of the “Investigations” record.

Goals
• Use spherical diffusion flames in long-duration mg 
environment to: 
– obtain experimental data of exceptional quality in 
simple, well-defined flow fields.
– understand various key elemental diffusion flame 
processes.
• Compare these data with those obtained through 
independent computational simulation with detailed 
chemistry and transport in order to:
– scrutinize and improve the accuracy and 
comprehensiveness of these descriptions.

s-Flame Merits of One-Dimensional Flames 
for Fundamental Studies
• Flame structure fundamentally affected by 
aerodynamics.
• Simple flow and flame configuration facilitate 
experimentation, computation, analysis, and 
comparison, with enhanced accuracy and reliability.
• Reduced effort in describing flows allows more 
detailed study of other aspects of flames such as 
chemistry.
• A one-dimensional flame is the simplest possible 
configuration.

• Burner generation assures

conditions.

s-Flame
II. Flame Extinction: 
Experimental, Low Da
• Fuel/inert mixtures will be issued from the spherical burner and 
ignited at initial flow rates expected (or known/observed) to form 
flames that evolve toward idealized steady-state conditions
• Following ignition and initial flame front movement, the fuel/inert 
flow rate will be abruptly reduced to a second flow rate below the 
expected extinction limit
• Quasi-steady extinction is expected to occur as the flame adjusts to 
the reduced flow rate
• To refine the determination of the extinction flow rate for each 
fuel/diluent mixture, repeated tests are to be conducted at 
successively lower initial flow rates and higher secondary flow 
rates.

title: s-Flame SCR 200802
text:
14
14
s-Flame II. Flame Extinction: 
Experimental, High Da
• Fuel/inert mixtures will be issued from the spherical burner 
and ignited at flow rates slightly above and beyond that of 
the radiation extinction limit.
• Upon ignition the flame will grow and subsequently 
extinguish at the radiation extinction limit. 
• Rates of radiative emissions from the flame and radiative 
reabsorption elsewhere are to be accentuated in some cases 
by using a radiatively active diluent such as CO2.

s-Flame III. Flamefront Instabilities: 
Phenomenology
• Stoichiometry constraint and lack of chemistry render 
diffusion flame sheets absolutely stable.
• However, chemistry becomes important for near-limit 
burning. Will flame become unstable? 
• Recent theories & experiments show instability 
characteristics similar to those of premixed flames for 
near-limit burning
• Since (positive) stretch suppresses cellular instability 
while promotes pulsating instability, the (stretchless) 
spherical flame is well suited for such studies.

and limit; also allows for extinction

The Role of mg Spherical Diffusion Flame in 
Comprehensive Mechanism Development
• Substantial research on homogeneous systems (shock 
tubes, flow reactors, etc.) and premixed flames

and stagnation flows, and droplet flames

Experimental Approach (2/6)
• Objective A – Flame Structure Evolution
–Fuel/diluent mixtures will be issued from the spherical 
burner and ignited at flow rates expected to form flames 
that evolve toward idealized steady-state conditions.
–As the flame spreads outward, transient measurements of 
flame front velocity and flame structure will be obtained 
using imaging and radiometric systems. 
–The flame characteristics will be compared with the 
predictions of the transient numerical simulation of 
spherical diffusion flames for evaluations of detailed 
chemical kinetic and transport models.

title: s-Flame SCR 200802
text:
40
40
s-Flame
Experimental Approach (3/6)
• Objective B – Quasi-Steady Extinction Limits, Low Da
– Fuel/inert mixtures will be issued from the spherical burner and 
ignited at initial flow rates expected (or known/observed) to 
form flames that evolve toward idealized steady-state conditions. 
– Following ignition and initial flame front movement, the 
fuel/inert flow rate will be abruptly reduced to a second flow 
rate below the expected extinction limit. 
– Quasi-steady extinction is expected to occur as the flame adjusts 
to the reduced flow rate. 
– To refine the determination of the extinction flow rate for each 
fuel/diluent mixture, repeated tests are to be conducted at 
successively lower initial flow rates and higher secondary flow 
rates.

title: s-Flame SCR 200802
text:
41
41
s-Flame
Experimental Approach (4/6)
• Objective B – Quasi-Steady Extinction Limits, Low Da
–At the low Da extinction limit, chemical kinetic rates are 
retarded with respect to flow rates by inert gas in the 
fuel stream that decreases the flame temperature.
–Based on theoretical predictions, fuel/inert mixtures are 
to be chosen for which the extinction flame radius is 
large enough to minimize the effects of heat loss to the 
burner.
–The surface temperature of the burner will be directly 
measured to quantify this loss.

title: s-Flame SCR 200802
text:
42
42
s-Flame
Experimental Approach (5/6)
• Objective B – Quasi-Steady Extinction Limits, High Da
–Fuel/inert mixtures will be issued from the spherical 
burner and ignited at flow rates above and beyond those 
expected (or known/observed) to form steady flames 
when radiative loss is considered. 
–The quasi-steady extinction is expected to occur as the 
flame moves outward before reaching the adiabatic
steady-state radius.
–Rates of radiative emissions from the flame and radiative 
reabsorption elsewhere are to be accentuated in some 
cases by using a radiatively active diluent such as CO2.

title: s-Flame SCR 200802
text:
43
43
s-Flame
Experimental Approach (6/6)
• Objective C – Flame Front Instabilities
–Pulsating flame front instabilities are predicted to occur 
near the extinction conditions at both low and high Da.
–The approach taken to observe the instabilities is similar to 
the approach for observing extinction except fuel/diluent 
mixtures with large system Lewis numbers (Le) are used.
• Low Da: moderate initial flow rate, abrupt change to flow rate 
below predicted extinction rate.
• High Da: initial flow rate above predicted extinction flow rate 
with radiation.
• Instabilities are expected to appear before extinction.
–Radiating diluents are used to further encourage the 
instabilities.
